#3000. Telegram issues security warning to iPhone users running older iOS versions

Messaging platform Telegram is sending out alerts to users running outdated versions of iOS, urging them to install the latest available software update. Here are the details.

Over the past few months, Apple has released multiple iOS updates to address security vulnerabilities, amid the growing use of AI tools to discover security flaws and develop exploits.

Throughout this year, Apple has also stepped up the frequency of its iOS security releases across multiple generations of the operating system.

Based on the company’s security releases page, Apple has issued iOS updates with published security advisories on 13 separate dates so far this year, up from 12 during the same period in 2025 and nine in 2024.

The number of vulnerabilities addressed in those updates has also increased considerably. Apple’s iOS security advisories list fixes for 707 distinct vulnerabilities affecting the iPhone so far this year, more than double the 334 Apple addressed in all of 2025. In 2024, that figure was 302.

In other words, Apple has addressed more iOS vulnerabilities so far this year than in 2024 and 2025 combined.

Granted, Apple is now issuing security updates for more generations of iOS than it was last year, but the company itself confirmed back in June that it was accelerating the rollout of security fixes in response to the growing capabilities of AI-powered hacking tools.

Additionally, Apple has issued at least two waves of mercenary spyware threat notifications over the past few months, reaching targeted users in 110 countries in August and 99 countries in late October.

Now, Telegram is issuing security warnings of its own.

In a post on X yesterday, Telegram founder and CEO Pavel Durov claimed that “iPhone users are being hacked on a massive scale,” noting that “just opening a website can be enough to get you hacked.”

For this reason, he said, Telegram has been sending out a security alert to all of its users running older versions of iOS, urging them to update their iPhones.

🚨 iPhone users are being hacked on a massive scale.If your iOS is even slightly outdated, all your data is at risk.Just opening a website can be enough to get you hacked.We're sending this warning to all our users on older iOS versions: pic.twitter.com/k2BKf5N5ua

Durov didn’t elaborate on the nature or extent of the alleged attacks, nor did he specify which iOS vulnerabilities were being exploited. That said, Apple addressed more than 30 WebKit vulnerabilities with the release of iOS 27.2 in late October alone, some of which could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code through maliciously crafted web content.

To be clear, Apple did not indicate that any of those vulnerabilities had been actively exploited.

As of this writing, the latest available versions of iOS for actively supported iPhones are iOS 27.2.1, iOS 26.7.3, and iOS 18.7.12, depending on which iOS generation your device is compatible with or currently running.

#2999. This Is the Biggest Change to Social Security in 2027 That Retirees Need to Know About

A new calendar year always brings changes to Social Security.

By Bram Berkowitz – Nov 28, 2026 at 10:49AM EST

For tens of millions of Americans, Social Security plays a critical role in supporting them in retirement. According to the Social Security Administration (SSA), nearly 71.8 million people receive benefits, and about 87% of Americans 65 and older collect them.

Furthermore, roughly 40% of beneficiaries age 65 and older get more than half their income from Social Security, and about 1 in 7 get more than 90%. An AARP survey this year found Social Security is the main source of income for half of recipients age 50 and older.

That's why one number the SSA announces each October is so critical. It determines how much monthly Social Security checks will rise each year. This is the biggest change to Social Security for 2027.

Each year, there is a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) to benefits in order to help Social Security checks keep pace with inflation, so retirees can maintain their purchasing power.

The SSA doesn't choose the raise. By law, it compares the average of the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) for July, August, and September of each year to the same number a year earlier. The percentage difference is the following year's COLA, and COLAs cannot be negative.

The SSA announced in October that the 2027 COLA will be 3.6%. For the average retired worker, the SSA estimates the monthly check will climb from $2,095 to $2,170 in January. That's an extra $75 a month, or about $900 a year.

It's the biggest raise since the 8.7% adjustment in 2023, and it tops each of the last three COLAs: 3.2% in 2024, 2.5% in 2025, and 2.8% in 2026. Over a longer stretch, the average adjustment since automatic COLAs began in 1975 is roughly 3.8%, so 3.6% is close to the long-term norm, but well above the majority of COLAs in the 21st century.

So why the bigger-than-normal number? Earlier in the year, many forecasters expected inflation to cool, which suggested a smaller COLA. Then the war with Iran sent energy prices soaring.

By September, overall energy costs were up about 20% from a year earlier, and those costs spilled into other categories. The Senior Citizens League's (TSCL) COLA forecast was only 2.8% in April.

The increase will certainly help, but it won't necessarily make retirees whole. TSCL estimates that benefits have lost about 13.7% of their buying power since 2016.

Critics argue that part of the problem is that the CPI-W tracks the spending of working households, while older Americans spend more of their budgets on healthcare, whose costs have tended to rise faster. In an AARP survey earlier this year, more than three-quarters of recipients said the projected 2027 COLA, which at the time was 3.5%, would be enough to keep pace with rising prices.

A bigger COLA can often be a double-edged sword. It's based on inflation data, so although benefits are rising, everyday items are likely to cost more.

And part of the raise will be eaten up by increases in Medicare premiums. The standard monthly Part B premium will rise by $6.50 to $209.40 in 2027, and the deductible will climb by $9 to $292. For the average retiree who pays the standard premium, that trims the $75 monthly increase to about $68.50.

With the new COLA in mind, retirees should start building their 2027 budgets, but be cautious about treating higher benefits as more discretionary income. Before planning additional discretionary purchases, factor in potentially higher costs for groceries, utilities, insurance, and healthcare in 2027, and make sure the increase is enough to cover them in your budget.

In an effort to cut costs, Samsung is postponing the launch of the Galaxy Watch 10, according to reports. Here's what to know.

You might have to wait over a year to get the Samsung Galaxy Watch 10: Samsung will not release any new Galaxy smartwatch in 2027, South Korea’s ET News reported on Sunday.

In an effort to cut costs after two quarters of consecutive losses and amid global RAM shortages, Samsung Electronics’ Mobile Business division will switch from an annual release schedule to a biannual one for its smartwatches, according to ET News. The switch follows other cost-cutting measures that will reduce production of the tech giant’s midrange smartphone lineup while increasing its premium Galaxy S27 offerings.

I am not mad at this decision by Samsung. Annual smartwatch updates are usually iterative anyway. Take Apple, for example. Its Apple Watch Series 10, released in 2024, had the same chip as the Apple Watch Series 11, released a year later. The most recent Apple Watch, the Apple Watch Series 12, has the same battery life as the Apple Watch Series 11. I’d expect Apple to keep its new sensors, which debuted on the Series 12 and Ultra 4, for its Series 13 or Ultra 5 next year.

Samsung’s Galaxy Watch 9, which debuted with a different chip and added a few more hours of battery, had the same bones as the Galaxy Watch 8.

If some of the biggest features on these smartwatches remain the same for a few years, why not change the release schedule to a biannual one?

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 vs. Galaxy Watch 8: I’ve compared both models, here’s my advice

Some of the most substantial updates that arrive on new devices like the Galaxy Watch 9 or Apple Watch Series 12 normally arrive through software updates, which end up landing on previous watch generations upon launch as well.

By switching from an annual release cycle to a biannual one, Samsung could drum up more excitement and anticipation between launches, and be able to surprise its customers with more purchase-worthy updates.

Samsung did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Anyone in the US who bought an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPhone 16 model between June 2024 and March 2025 is eligible to file a claim.

The last day to file a claim in Apple’s $250 million settlement over delayed Siri features is Dec. 21, and payouts could reach $95 per eligible iPhone.

The class covers anyone in the US who bought an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or any iPhone 16 model between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, the stretch when Apple was promoting a more personal Siri that hadn’t arrived yet. Filing takes a few minutes online, and each qualifying phone gets its own claim.

The iPhone 16 went on sale in September 2024 with Apple Intelligence at the center of its marketing. However, the first AI features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, several weeks later, and the most heavily promoted one, a Siri that could pull personal context from your apps, was further delayed in March 2025.

Now you can turn that initial dismay into a payment in Apple’s $250 million legal settlement by signing up at a live website. The opt-in form is available only for a limited time, so get your name in the pool before it closes. Eligible buyers have until Dec. 21 to file, and each qualifying iPhone gets its own claim.

Apple settled a false advertising lawsuit brought by Clarkson Law Firm in May, agreeing to pay $250 million to customers who bought some iPhone models during a specified period. The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled customers by promising AI features that didn’t ship with the new devices. Apple denies all of the lawsuit’s allegations and denies that it did anything unlawful or improper.

If you purchased an iPhone 16 or iPhone 15 at launch, you may be entitled to receive a portion of the quarter-billion-dollar settlement. Payouts between $25 and $95 per eligible device are expected.

“Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” an Apple spokesperson said in an earlier statement to CNET.

The court granted preliminary approval of the settlement on July 17. Then an Aug. 13 order moved up the final approval date by seven months.

“False advertising settlements aim to raise the floor of truth-telling, protect fair competition and increase consumer choice,” said Ryan Clarkson, co-lead counsel on the case and founder and managing partner of Clarkson Law Firm, in a statement to CNET. He claimed it’s the largest false-advertising settlement in history.

Apple lit up its flagship New York City store to resemble Siri’s new color scheme.

As of Sept. 21, you can go to SmartphoneAISettlement.com and enter your information to confirm your eligibility for monetary relief. People whom Apple and the settlement administrator determined would be eligible will also receive email or postal notices from the company Verita directing them to the website.

The claims window closes on Dec. 21, 2026, so you have three months to act.

If you bought one of the following devices between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, you could be eligible to receive a settlement payment:

The iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max are included because they have the processor and memory to run Apple Intelligence features.

It’s estimated that approximately 36 million customers are eligible for this settlement.

When Apple advertised its new iPhone 16 lineup in 2024, it emphasized how the models were optimized for AI features such as an enhanced Siri that could act as an intelligent agent. When the phones did arrive, Apple Intelligence wasn’t yet ready; its first features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, five weeks later.

According to the proposed settlement, “Apple allegedly saturated the market with deceptive ads, inducing consumers to purchase iPhones based on the promise of certain enhanced Siri features.”

Some features of Apple Intelligence did ship soon after the introduction of the iPhone 16 and iOS 18, including Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji and Clean Up. But those weren’t the advanced features Apple highlighted. In fact, the type of intelligent interactions Apple advertised is only starting to show up in Siri AI, which is part of iOS 27, which was released in early September.

According to the settlement, Apple needed to provide the information about affected customers within five days of the settlement approval. As of late July, preliminary approval has been granted by the court.

After the data is provided and verified, a 45-day notice period begins to inform potential consumers that they’re eligible for a payment.

On Aug. 13, US District Court Judge Noël Wise granted approval to push forward the date from Sept. 29, 2027, to Feb. 24, 2027.

Provided approval is granted, the first checks or deposits will arrive sometime within a 60-day window after February next year, depending on court dates and possible extensions.

#2993. How Bonds Shaped the Course of Human History

The history of the bond market is a centuries-long story of wars, empires, innovations, manias, and an interesting cast of characters.

By Motley Fool Staff – Nov 28, 2026 at 11:00AM EST

In this episode of Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing, Motley Fool personal finance expert Robert Brokamp discusses the intersection of human history and bond history with Robin Wigglesworth, the editor of the Financial Times' finance blog Alphaville, and the author of a new book, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic Story of How Bonds Built the Modern World. Robert and Robin discuss:

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

This podcast was recorded on Nov. 14, 2026.

Robert Brokamp: How bonds built the modern world this week on the Personal Finance Edition of the Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing Podcast. I'm Robert Brokamp though I go by the nickname of Bro. Let's face it. Many people find bonds boring. After all, there's a reason Ian Fleming gave his fictional spy the last name of Bond. He called it the "dullest name I've ever heard." However, dig into the history of bonds, and you will find that it is a centuries-long story of wars, empires, innovations, fear, greed, and an interesting cast of characters. Here to talk to us about the intersection of human history and bond history is Robin Wigglesworth, the editor of the Financial Times Finance blog Alphaville and the author of a fascinating and dare I say rollicking new book A Fabulous Debt: The Epic Story of How Bonds Built the Modern World. Robin, welcome to the show.

Robin Wigglesworth: Thanks for having me on, Bro. I've been looking forward to it.

Robert Brokamp: So your book covers many ways that bonds funded big events and developments over the course of history. But I have to say that my first impression after reading, particularly the first third or so of the book, is that bonds funded a lot of wars or defense, depending on how you look at it. This includes the very first bond market in Venice. Let's start with that story. Tell us about how bonds got birthed in Italy.

Robin Wigglesworth: Yes, I can't remember which Greek philosopher that first said that war is the mother and father of all invention, but it's certainly true for pretty much everything, but certainly in the financial realm, war has been brought out the worst and the best in human ingenuity. This is the 12th century. Venice is a weird city. Have you been there, Bro?

Robert Brokamp: I have, indeed. It's beautiful, and I was just struck at how, frankly, very focused on mercantilism. It occurred to me, reading your book, that it’s been that way for centuries.

Robin Wigglesworth: I visited once when I was a feckless student, essentially, and I wish I appreciated the history more because it's a unique city. It was founded by refugees fleeing the Vandals, basically some Visigoths, German barbarians. They settled where they settled because nobody else wanted it. It was a swampy hellhole. It had zero natural resources, no farm there, no nothing. So they were left to piece there. They realized they had to live off their wits. The Venetians became really the Mediterranean's most brilliant merchants, the traders. They were well positioned between East and West, so they had no natural resources, but they were very smart. They were very cunning, very driven, very ambitious. They were perfectly positioned between East and West. They were technically part of the Byzantine Empire, based in Constantinople, today's Istanbul, but they're also part of Italy, of course, and they owed some fealty to the pope, but essentially their only loyalty was to money. They liked making money.

It was one of those rare places where there was lots of social mobility, as well. There's Djers who roll the town that you literally go within several generations, go from being a slave to being the head of the city. If you were good enough at business, that's really the only thing that mattered. But this really annoyed everybody else in Europe at the time. These are the nouveau-up petty merchants. Nobody likes merchants. So they ended up in war with Constantinople at one point, their liege, and they needed a ton of money. To fight that war, walls are very expensive and more money than they could just borrow from the local banks. Already banks in the way that we understand, but local money lenders. They were called banks or bunkie because of the wooden tables they had. They therefore forced everybody in the town to pay a proportional wealth tax, essentially. They assessed everybody's wealth and made them pay a forcible loan to the government. To soften the blow, it was a republic. To soften the blow, they made it a loan, paid 5% a year, and made the receipts tradable. That was the crucial bit.

Robert Brokamp: Yeah, because loans have been around for centuries before then. It was the tradable part that was important because it then became a financial asset and you had people with both liabilities and assets that were the key to its success, and it gave a sense of especially the more affluent people feeling like they had a stake in what was going on.

Robin Wigglesworth: Yeah, there are so the magical bit that I hadn't quite appreciated before doing the research on a fabulous debt was how bonds quite literally have bound countries, states, cities, people, the governed, and the government together. Venice lost that war against Constantinople. The Doge was murdered by his own citizens on the streets of Venice for his sins. This loan, this in theory, temporary war loan became a permanent debt. But, in fact, that proved a blessing because the Venetians because they were great merchants, they realized, "It's really valuable. You can buy an income stream." Venice couldn't repay the loan, but it could keep paying the 5% from the taxes it raised, from its customs duties, and so on, and being able to buy an income stream was hugely powerful. You could sell that income stream, as well. Then, therefore, you could use it as collateral for trade. So it became like money. In a world that was always desperately short of something that people accepted as money. Venetian bonds were broadly accepted around the world because Venice was good for it. Therefore, this monument is the failure of the Venetians or this embarrassing war became a monument to their commercial genius, really. It was incredible, and then you saw the other Italian city-states quickly copied this invention, and it spread around Europe and took off from there.

Robert Brokamp: Your book is not only a history of bonds, but to a certain degree, a history of which countries were more powerful, which countries had empires. There's a bit about Spain and its empire, and one of the subjects of that empire was the Netherlands. But eventually, they were to get their independence with the help of bonds. Tell us a little bit about Dutch finance.

Robin Wigglesworth: Yeah, though the bond, the prestiti was called in Italy, spread around Europe. Everybody copied it because people were always keen to borrow. But I think it was really the Dutch that first created what we'd understand to be a bond market. In that, there were lots of different issuers. The Dutch first used it to finance the incredibly elaborate system of dikes they built to keep their country dry. Then over the time, cities, provinces, towns, villages would issue more and more bonds, and they'd lend to each other. So people in Amsterdam would buy Utrecht bonds and vice versa. Ultimately, when they also invented the first listed public company, the Dutch East India Company also issued the first corporate bonds. So they'd issue bonds to finance their activities.

The Dutch first then financed their war for independence against Spain at the time, with bonds. They could fund themselves almost to infinity and beyond at 3% a year, whilst the Spanish crown was infamous for defaulting. Philip II defaulted, I think, three or four times in his life, which is a world record, which you have to respect. He's the goated sovereign debt defaulter in history. Because of that, Spain just had to periodically deal with its finances, whilst the Dutch could keep on fighting. They won independence, and then they built the global empire actually on the back of bonds. The Dutch East India Company only sold shares once, but its activities, its colonies, its chips, its soldiers were financed by bond sales. That’s why I think the Dutch managed to evolve from what people, slightly cruelly but not inaccurately, called the bog of Europe to be one of the great powers in the world, really.

Robert Brokamp: Your book then moves on to other empires, including the British Empire and the consul market. I think one of the interesting aspects of the book is that you address how people react to the debt. In fact, the title of the book comes from a book written in 1848 by Thomas Babington Macaulay. I hope I'm pronouncing that right. There were a lot of people who were decrying the high levels of debt. I think you labeled them debt scolds and saying that bankruptcy and ruin were at hand, but that didn't happen. Instead, Macaulay argued that a bond market could actually be an economic boon, which is why he called it a fabulous debt. What do the debt scolds get wrong or did they get wrong?

Robin Wigglesworth: Well, actually, a lot of the arguments that Thomas Babington Macaulay was countering, you can see to this very day. First of all, it's the conflation of household debt with government debt. It's a classic mistake, but a government is not a country. There are aspirations around it. Every country is different, every financial system is different. We don't borrow money from Mars or Venus. We borrow money from ourselves. That's why he thought that obvious that naked obsession with just the nominal level of the debt is a distraction. What I think Thomas Babington Macaulay also captured so brilliantly is that a national debt can also be a national blessing, to steal the wording of another character in my book, because you can use it as collateral, you can use it to lubricate trade, you can use it to grease commerce. Really, credit, as you said, predates everything else in finance. It predates money.

Credit has pretty much always been around with us, and it is the countries that use credit to get commerce flowing that tends to be richer, they tend to be more successful. They tend to therefore also be more powerful. Thomas Babington Macaulay saw that the massive debts that Britain had gradually incurred fighting so many wars in Europe because there was always a war. Actually, it had not led to the Bron of Britain. In fact, Britain had gotten richer and richer and richer every time. It would occasionally pay down some of those debts, and then there'd be a new war and then inflate again. But broadly speaking, this actually was an asset to Britain, not a curse. That's why I still think to this day that, it wouldn't be human not to worry occasionally about debt levels and how much debt governments today have incurred. But I also think it's important to remember the nuances that this is not a household and debt can be a tool. It can be abused, but broadly speaking, it's arguably the most valuable social technology we've invented. Certainly the most valuable financial technology we've invented.

Robert Brokamp: You mentioned earlier that the bond market could actually bind a society or a country together, which brings us to the start of the United States, which in 1783, the Treaty of Paris was signed. The new country had an awful lot of debt. In comes Alexander Hamilton, the first head of the newly created Treasury Department. What did he do that set America up for success?

Robin Wigglesworth: Did you notice how I did the foreshadowing there and said talk about a national blessing? Yeah, quite happy about how I did that. So Alexander Hamilton was, I think, an incandescent genius. We know he was brilliant, but I think having now read some of his papers, his letters, not just the biographies, but some of the underlying writings, it is incredible how prescient he was. He had studied the British financial system whilst he was still fighting in the Revolutionary War and had realized that Britain's sea of credit was not a weakness as many other Americans thought. It was actually a source of Britain's strength. He suggested ways that maybe America would try to weaken it.

But when he became the first treasury secretary, his first job apart from hiring two assistants and getting one emergency loan from a bank in Philadelphia was to present a report to Congress about what to do with all the debts that the various states or the colonies until then had incurred in fighting this war. That was a mix of greenbacks and dollars, basically currency continental dollars, continentals that they'd issued, and bonds they sold both to American investors and to overseas investors, primarily in France and the Netherlands. I think his genius was realizing that this problem actually could solve two problems at Watts. He couched this very much in terms of, This is the price of liberty. We want to be seen as a serious country, hold our head up aloft among all the other serious countries in the world, and serious countries, they pay their debts. These were debts we incurred, fighting for liberty, we have to pay it. We will restore America's credit worthiness, and be respected by other countries. That was one of the main public rationales.

Two other ones were more subtle. One is, I think he also realized that credit or these bonds by taking responsibility for all the state debts, Washington it wasn't Washington then, but, like, the new federal government in New York at the time, could issue new bonds, and those bonds, as long as they were current, would get treated like money. That was hugely important in a country where the economy was a shambles. It had been wrecked by the war. It was cut off from its biggest trading partner, Britain, pretty much its only trading partner. It was a desperate shortage of anything that looked, hooked, and quack like money. These bonds, and there's a great line actually in the musical, which mentions this obliquely. But Alexander Hamilton raps in the musical. This will be a financial enema for the American economy, which is quite evocative right. But very true, and that's how it functioned. I think the third reason is this binding issue that you mentioned. I hadn't found any evidence he studied the Venetians, but he'd studied the Dutch as well, and he saw that by lending to each other, you can bind countries together.

In Venice, for example, once you borrowed money from your citizens, the town or the city, well, the citizens had a vested interest in your good governance. But also vested interest in your continued survival. Same thing with the Dutch, Dutch towns became a country by lending to each other. Britain, again, also became a United Kingdom by setting up a consolidated annuities market, it's called the Consol Market, World's first treasury bonds, really. He saw that with a very, very vulnerable, weak federal government and he wanted a strong one, you could actually give all Americans that also held this debt a vested interest in the federal government surviving by making them creditors. By exchanging all these defaulted bonds in new fresh printed, well, not printed at the time, but fresh treasury bonds, you could actually give the federal government a fighting chance.

Because now we think of history as a series of natural and inescapable conclusions, B follows A and C follows B. History doesn't work that way. It's just a series of accidents. It was not written in the stars that America would become the mighty country it is. There were 13 squabbling colonies that didn't always get on, and it was not assured that it would emerge as one country or stay as one country. In fact, there was a civil war, of course, later. But I think a lot of the steps Alexander Hamilton made in those first fateful few years were hugely impactful in binding the country together, healing the economy, and restoring America's credit around the world. [MUSIC]

Robert Brokamp: Nowadays, we're talking a lot about the AI build-out and the increasing role that bonds are playing. When people look back at history for maybe a comparable period, some have suggested the build-out of the railroads, which you cover in your book. Tell us about how Bonds built the rails and led to one of the worst economic downturns in U.S. history.

Robin Wigglesworth: Yes, it was a humdinger. I love traveling by rail. I'd much rather travel by rail anytime I can, so that chapter was fun. We think of rail as a very everyday, old-fashioned transportation now, but it was a revolutionary technology. It was hard to fathom for us today how awestruck people were at this new invention and the impact it had. Everything from the AI fears we have today, people feared that the railway that the human body wasn't built for these mad cap speeds. There were lots of newspapers that write about people going mad at speeds over 30 miles an hour. At 40-50 miles, I think, they feared the body might disintegrate. Because is humans weren't built for those sort of magical speeds. But everywhere in the world went railway mad. Britain, of course, started, but it spread around Europe, Tsarist Russia, even China, but nowhere on the planet went as railway mad as Americans because it was the perfect lab for it. It was the mix of America's can-do dreaming spirit. A country that was vast in geography, but quite sparsely populated and quite spread out and quite Balkanized, as well. Also, they started building railways before the Civil War. But after the Civil War became a very potent symbol of unifying the country after this horrific Civil War. The transcontinental railways became this potent sign of America and its belief in the future.

These were like in A Fabulous Debt, I call them like a series of Apollo programs, these kind of big titanic civilizational missions, and that's how they were seen. But unfortunately, they were almost all financed by debt. There were railway stocks as well, and there were people would sign, paid locals in the town would finance it by signing up for shares. But the vast majority of the financing came from the bond market. Because the American banking system was a bit of a mess. There was no federal reserve then. There was no central bank. It was just a series of very small state by state banks that would collapse very quickly. Bonds finance a lot of it and people went a little bit mad. Foreigners also chuck money at the American bond market, the railway bond market. They were financing everything. The Dutch, Brits, Germans, Austrians, Spanish, everybody would buy railway bonds, American railway bonds. In 1873, ironically, it wasn't really America's fault, though, there were all sorts of scandals around the railways. There was so much corruption. Even the vice president was implicated at one point. People are worried about the railway boom.

But there was a financial crisis in Europe, here, in Germany and Austria that essentially caused massive stock market drop in Germany and Austria, that cause all these European investors. As you know, in a crisis, you don't sell what you want to sell, you sell what you can sell. They sold American railway bonds. Then suddenly, you had a series of American banks were in extremely precarious position because the prices of these bonds were cratering. They had them on the balance sheet, and primarily there was this one bank called Jay Cooke and Co., or Cooke and Co. He was the John Pierpont Morgan of his era. He was the giant financier that had helped bankroll the North to victory in the Civil War. He was the most famous, most powerful man in American business at the time. His bank went belly up. The shock must have been incredible. There's all sort of newspaper reports about the panic that gripped New York when this happened when they literally barred the doors because that's how a bank would basically say, we're shut for business, you can't pull your money out.

But it's a bit like if JP Morgan today suddenly said, Oh, we're bankrupt. That's how big a shock it was. Then that financial crisis, everything collapsed, and that ricocheted back in Europe, and you have a classic thing where things start feeding on themselves. It was for a long time called The Great Depression until we actually had the Great Depression. Now we call it typically the Long Recession or the long depression because it’s still the longest economic downturn in American history, and it was all because railway bonds were the real culprit there.

Robert Brokamp: It's another example of how there can be overinvestment; there can be a mania; there can be a bubble. But in the end, what came out on the other end was still very beneficial.

Robin Wigglesworth: Yeah, I mean, it's a great point, isn't it? Financial crises are no fun. I've lived through 1.5 or 2.5, depending on I wasn't old enough to remember some of them. They are destructive and socially debilitating, but they are probably unavoidable. Quite often, that kind of mania, one of the things I often like to say is that the optimal number of financial crises is not zero, that we occasionally need investors to take leave of their senses to dream. Not worry about what could go wrong, but think of all the amazing things that could go right. Because they pour money into new technologies, and quite often they lose money. Sometimes they lose so much money, it causes a financial crisis. But quite often what they finance, that's how we make these big leaps forward. The railways is an amazing example. This made America a superpower. It was not recognized in America at the time. It was only really seen by world, the contours of it by World War I, so 50 years after this big crash. But the railway system became this physical skeleton of the American economy, transformed America. I think you cannot underestimate how impactful it was in creating the United States of America we know today. Yes it, to use the technical word, sucked for a few years, and lots of people lost a lot of money. But long term, these manias are actually quite good for society as a whole, not always, but most of the time.

Robert Brokamp: Your book is an interesting history of how things used to be. Not really all that long ago. I think a good example of that is the rise of money market funds.

Robert Brokamp: So tell us the story of Bruce Bent and Henry Brown and the conditions of the 1960s that led to the creation of the modern money market fund, which I guess starts with a Depression era law known as Regulation Q.

Robin Wigglesworth: Yeah. I often paraphrase one of my favorite bands from when I was younger, Wu-Tang Clan. That said, "Cash rules everything around us." Sorry. I said, financial arbitrage rules everything around us. The US, after World War II and afterward, had something called Regulation Q that regulated how much interest you could get in a bank account. If you're a big institution, a big company or very wealthy person, you could buy treasury bonds. They paid a high interest rate. You could buy lots of things that would pay you above inflation interest rates. But most people were stuck in deposit accounts, that paid, far below inflation. They invented the first money market fund. But basically, using the mutual fund technology is a way of pooling lots of money so they could buy treasury bills, bonds, commercial paper, ASPAC commercial paper, certificates of deposit, the whole thing. Really to democratize access to some of these products that wealthy people and companies will already have access to. I think it was a hugely valuable thing.

Then the money market funds eventually morphed into something almost like if think of credit as the lifeblood for any sort of real economy, the money market funds, especially in America, is the bloodstream of the blood that goes through the US financial system. Because they grew so big, so quickly. Even when Regulation Q was scrapped, it just became a huge part of the American financial industry. It basically bailed out a lot of asset managers in the '70s and '80s when there really struggling. It was growth of mutual funds. Money market funds really helped, like, Vanguard survive many lean years in the '80s. Fidelity, as well, might not have been around if they didn't have the money market fund franchise. Now it's this dark force that binds the entire financial system together. It's what $7-8 trillion just in the United States. It's how vast amounts of finance and financial transactions gets lubricated every day. It's really a financial wonder of the world.

Robert Brokamp: What I love about the story is that first of all, it's the vision of two guys sharing an office. One had to basically put a second mortgage on his home for the business to continue. It succeeds. They have the oldest money market fund, but the reserve primary fund, but in the end, that didn't come to such a great ending.

Robin Wigglesworth: No, it's quite tragic, actually. You want to root for the pioneers. I like that this was an independent money market fund complex. They were hugely successful. They were copied by everybody else who had, like, these vast asset management groups like Fidelity and State Street. But they were the plucky outside or the plucky pioneer. They were, for a long time, exceptionally conservative. The two founders felt that money market funds should be conservative. This is all about capital protection and making it work a little bit from you, but being careful. But as money market funds started buying commercial paper, and then ultimately, so this is short term IOUs issued by big companies like IBM or GE they also started buying asset backed commercial paper, which the short term IOUs that investment banks use to lubricate their securitization engines before 2008.

That was a bit of a disaster. The first reserve fund famously, one of the founders said that I don't do drugs, I don't do booze, I don't cheat, and I don't buy commercial paper or something that was to that effect. They were very conservative, very long, but they eventually obviously lost market share. This is just a tragedy that you see happen again and again. Even as I was researching this, and I could see where things were heading, I was almost shouting to myself, please don't do it, don't do it and then they did it. Literally in 2007, they take out a line from the prospectus where they say, we don't buy commercial paper and started buying commercial paper. Then, first, we're exposed to some of the Bear Stearns funds that first went belly up in the summer of 2007. Then more problematic, they were extremely exposed to Bear Stearns itself, when they went belly up in March 2008. But Bear got bailed out by JP Morgan, which had basically the Federal Reserve pushing them together, but by the time Lehman went under. They still hadn't gotten out of it. They still basically been trying to squeeze more and more yield out, had been lending more and more risky stuff, and they lost money when Lehman went under. Obviously, in dollar terms, the loss was not big, but they broke the buck. [inaudible] their net asset value went below one, and to many people in the stock market or bond market world, that sounds inconsequential. Like, you've lost 0.02% of your money.

But of course, this is not where you're supposed to lose money. This is supposed to be the financial equivalent of a steel vault. Obviously, it causes this incentive that you want to get out. It's a bank run incentive. Because if you can get out quickly, you can get out at the NAB [inaudible] quite often. But of course, that causes everybody to rush for the exit because they want to get their money at first from the bank. That's what happened and the first reserve fund basically suddenly had. When Lehman went bust and they broke the buck, they had, I think, something like $40 billion of outflows. It's like an electronic bank run in a matter of a few days, and they acted, gate and shut, and that just paralyzed the entire industry. Because so much of the financial machinery depends on money market funds to lubricate things. Things were not good in September of 2008, either. It forced the government to basically bail out the entire industry. They didn't send the money, but they basically said, look, it's better for us to just guarantee all money market funds.

We guarantee that the federal government stands behind all of them to prevent this already cataclysmic event, escalating into, I guess, being Norwegian, something I call a financial Ragnarock. It would have been horrifically bad. 2008 was bad. If the money market fund industry had been allowed to collapse, it would have been immeasurably worse. It would quite possibly have been something like the Great Depression [inaudible].

Robert Brokamp: Your book talks a lot about, again, the benefits of the debt, but also has some of these stories of where too much debt was a problem. The final chapter of your book is titled How Much Is Too Much and you point out that if you add up all the world's debt, government, corporate banks, personal debt, we're like $340 trillion. In that chapter, you introduce something called Ferguson's Law. Tell us about the law and your answer to how much is too much.

Robin Wigglesworth: I think we're at 350 trillion now, so it's already gone up a bit since the book came out, since the book was edited, I guess. Ferguson’s law was coined by Neil Ferguson, the financial historian, but he actually dedicates it to an intellectual predecessor called Adam Ferguson, a Scottish philosopher who first said that debt was one of the main sources of ruin for all great nations. Neil Ferguson took that observation and turn it into an idea or suggestion or a thesis, or he calls it a law. That says that, when a country spends more on simply paying the interest on its debt than it does on defense, it tends to lead to decline. This is in the context of great powers, superpowers, but also great powers.

When England essentially was paying, had borrowed so much money after World War I, that it wasn't able to pay to maintain its empire, its military, its navy, and had to shrink, it tended to hasten that decline. It made the country poorer, and then it starts feeding on themselves. The reason why this is so resonant now is, America, for the first time in a century occasionally you can violate the law because you suddenly jack up interest payments because you're borrowing a lot of money or whatever, but America violated the Ferguson's law in 2024, two years ago, and is still in violation of it. Now, it's spending more just servicing its debts, not paying it down, just paying the interest than it does on its entire military.

Robert Brokamp: Given your review of the history of how debt has both contributed to the rise but also maybe the undermining of empires, what's your advice for America? There's no easy solution. Is it just you have to bite the bullet for a while and get it under control?

Robin Wigglesworth: Well, to paraphrase Warren Buffett, it's an easy solution. It's just very hard to do. The easy solution is to increase taxes a little bit and cut spending a little bit. America, I am actually, Brok, I'll bring you good news. I'm not that worried about America. I think the size of the economy, people stare too much at just the nominal size of the debt, 40 trillion. that is a scary amount of debt, and how quickly a lot of that has come just in the past 10, 20 years. Don't forget in the '90s, we remember, in the '90s. People were worried about the American financial system and how it would function with zero treasuries. America had such big budget deficits as recently as the late ‘90s that they stopped auctioning 30-year Treasuries, and people genuinely worried, like, how do things even work without Treasuries if America pays down all its debts? That obviously sounds like fancy land today. But it's just to show that things can change quite quickly. America still has an incredibly vibrant, dynamic economy and frankly, does not tax nearly as much as many other developed countries does.

In percent of GDP, America spends around 3.5% of its GDP on servicing its debts. That is almost mechanically going to go up because the budget deficit is huge and is not narrowed, and interest rates are higher now than they were, so it's refinanced. The US is constantly repaying treasuries it issued 10 years ago at 2% a year that now costs at 5% a year. It's just mechanically going to go up probably up to 4, 5%. That has been fine for many other countries before it. They're around 5%, it can start snowballing a bit. That's what we saw, for example, what happened in the UK. They hit 5% of the spend, 5% of GDP on servicing its stats in 1980. Then you had Margaret Thatcher came into power. She turned the ship around, things changed there. Canada, hilariously enough because we don't really think of Canada as financially profligate, but Canada had a huge debt problem. They spent 10% of GDP or 9.6% of GDP in the mid '90s. Then they had a bipartisan agreement to say, well, this is silly. It's just wasteful to spend so much financial of our budgets and our economic wealth on just paying our debts. There was a bipartisan agreement to cut spending and increase taxes. They did at a time when the economy was growing fairly well. The austerity was painful, but it was fine.

Within a few years, Canada had turned the financial ship around, and it went from AAA country to a single A country and back to AAA 'cause the grades that the credit rating agencies use. Those countries have the advantage that they borrow in British pounds or Canadian dollars. But I like Canadian dollars and I like British pounds. But the American dollar is unique. I think America has far more capacity to borrow than anybody else on the planet. Now, the downside of that, this is why I am a little bit worried about the US, on the other hand, because of that advantage, it makes America a little bit immune to all those other pressures that other countries can feel. Like the UK, in 2022, felt the heat of the bond market and they haven't turned the ship around, but at least they learned that they're in the danger zone and they need to get out of it. France is now butting up against that, as well. They're also getting a little bit worried about the bond market and that they might rebel. Canada also felt this a little bit the 1990s. But America, I just think, interest rates can go up, bond yields can go up, borrowing costs can go up. I just don't think they're going to go up as much enough to put enough pressure, what looks to me, if I'm being honest, like a fairly broken political system or struggles, that bipartisan agreement that you saw in Canada. I struggle. I'm not a political scientist, but I struggle to [inaudible] America today.

Therefore, the most likely outcome, I suspect, is that America totters on. There will be maybe some more budgetary discipline at some point. It'll wax and wane. Interest rates will go up. They'll go down. But over the next 10, 20 years, America's debt will keep inflating. With not enough pressure on the other side, no political will to increase taxes enough or cut spending enough, the debts will just keep on inflating for the next generation or two. Maybe at some point, there will be enough political will to change things. But I don't think it's going to happen anytime soon.

Robert Brokamp: I think one of the earliest tests of it will be when the Social Security Trust funds go bust in 2032 or so. At some point, there's going to have to be a hard choice there, and I think it'll test your theory of whether we can get enough bipartisan agreement to solve something.

Robin Wigglesworth: Yeah. I'm an optimist. I generally think that, by profession, I love bad news. I love financial crisis. It sounds horrific to say, but they are professionally fascinating. I get my rocks off with big crises. I am inherently cynical as a journalist. But as a human being, I actually think humans, things don't move in a straight line, and we mess up things all the time. But I actually do believe that at some point, America will feel, will look and say, well, look, we're spending 5% of GDP or 10% of the budget on just paying interest on our debt. That is silly. There are so many other things we want to spend money on. We want to spend more money on healthcare, education, AI data centers, rockets to the moon, to Mars, whatever and there will be some bipartisan agreement to cut spending and increase taxes. We're not talking about swinging to budget surplus tomorrow. That'd be economically devastating. But just getting the lines pointing in the right direction would not take that much effort. Getting them pointing forcefully in the right direction will take a bit of an effort, but one I think is entirely possible. But right now, feels hard to predict that it's going to happen anytime soon, but I think it'll be fine. Countries have had those positions with a pension savings. I think that's going to be quite difficult. Americans have triumphed through harder challenges than this, so I believe in you guys.

Robert Brokamp: Thank you, Robin. I appreciate that confidence, and I certainly hope that you are right. Well, congrats on the book. I really enjoyed it, and thanks so much for joining us.

Robin Wigglesworth: No, Bro, thanks so much for having me on and let me bang on about the bond market. It is my favorite subject in the whole world, as you can probably beat out.

Robert Brokamp: Yes. Thank you so much. That's the show. Thank you so much for spending part of your weekend with us, and thanks to Bart Shannon, as always, the engineer for this episode. #2991. The Winter Solstice Is Coming: A Guide to the Longest Night

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Next month, we'll experience the shortest daylight hours of the year.

This was taken with the main camera as a ProRaw photo. Notice the lights on the tree, compared to the green hue of the street lighting and blue and pink tones in the sky.

Thanksgiving is almost here, as is Cyber Monday, but soon it’ll be officially winter. The winter solstice is on Dec. 21, when we’ll experience Earth’s shortest, darkest day.

The winter solstice has a few different meanings, so here are all of them. The most common definition, and the one you’re most likely familiar with, is that it denotes the shortest day and longest night of the year on Earth. These times vary depending on your location on the globe, but the further north you live, the less sunlight you’ll get. In the tropics, they’ll get about 12 hours of sunlight. In Sweden, it’ll be closer to 6 hours. In Svalbard, there isn’t any.

The reason this occurs is due to the second definition of the winter solstice: During this time, the North Pole is tilted as far away from the sun as it can get. According to The Farmer’s Almanac, the moment at which the Earth’s axis is physically tilted as much as it can be is at 3:50 p.m. ET on Monday, Dec. 21. After that moment, the process will begin to reverse until the South Pole takes its turn during the summer solstice. At that point, the North Pole will be at its closest tilt to the sun, giving us the longest day and shortest night of the year for the Northern Hemisphere.

Sunset will occur at its earliest time on Dec. 21.

It’ll vary by location. The southern US will have the most sunlight, with Florida getting a little over 10 hours during the winter solstice. The Midwest and Great Lakes portion of the country will get roughly nine hours. The Pacific Northwest can expect a little less than nine hours. Southern Alaska will get about six hours, and the northern areas of Alaska will see around three hours.

If you want to see how your area will fare, Time and Date has a sunrise and sunset tool you can use. Input your zip code into the search bar, and you’ll be able to see your sunrise and sunset times.

The city of Utqiaġvik, Alaska, will have it worse than most in the US: It won’t get any sun at all. The sun won’t rise there again until late January. We hope the people living there packed their vitamin D supplements.

The autumn equinox was just a couple of months ago, so you may be curious about the differences. A solstice occurs when the Earth’s poles are tilted as far away from the sun as they’ll be over the course of one year, which is also one orbit around the sun. The equinoxes take place at the halfway points between each solstice. The autumn equinox takes place in September between the summer and winter solstices, while the spring equinox takes place in March between the winter and summer.

During an equinox, the poles are minimally tilted, and the days are as even as they can be. This also has a couple of other interesting side effects: The sun is pointed directly at the equator during an equinox, and the sun will rise and set directly east and west, respectively.

Humans use the solstices and equinoxes to mark the change of the seasons. There are two equinoxes and two solstices, which mark the start and end dates for Earth’s four seasons.

Decorating with evergreen trees, like with a wreath, is what they used to do to celebrate the winter solstice.

While the solstice is close to the holidays, celebrations for the winter solstice have been around for significantly longer, and some winter solstice traditions have become Christmas traditions as well. One of the most historically famous winter solstice celebrations is Yule, a winter festival originating thousands of years ago among the ancient Norse. It became commonly celebrated in Europe and involved bonfires and massive feasts. Yule celebrations also included decorating with evergreen tree decorations, like holly and ivy.

If these sound familiar, it’s because Christmas co-opted many of those traditions centuries ago, and the two traditions have kind of merged into a single seasonal holiday. The terms Yule and Christmas are often used interchangeably these days in many cultures.

So if you want to celebrate the winter solstice, just do all of the stuff you would normally do for the holidays. Burn a Yule log, decorate a tree, eat a big feast with your family and hang up mistletoe and wreaths — those are all hat tips to traditional winter solstice celebrations.

#2990. Claude can ship code for you now – how to try it (if you dare)

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Would you let a few Claude agents review and ship your code for you?

Developers are already using Claude Code and other AI-powered coding tools like OpenAI’s Codex in droves, but some still want to check code themselves before pushing it. A new feature from Anthropic is banking on more adventurous, agent-first coders being comfortable with handing even that last step off to AI.

With Claude Ship, announced in beta Monday, “Claude can now review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows,” Anthropic said. The feature is geared toward individual developers or companies who want to move faster or already delegate a significant amount of coding tasks to agents.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

“Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person,” Anthropic said. “The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

The new feature uses two new agents alongside Code Review, which Anthropic released in March for Teams and Enterprise plans. Code Review first collects, organizes, and posts findings to a PR. Then, Anthropic said, the agents, PR Steward and Claude Approvals, guide a PR “through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually.”

PR Steward can’t approve or merge pull requests, designed instead to participate “on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members.” It also documents what it changed in each push through comments and provides instructions for how to undo it, should developers want to. Throughout the process, developers can give Claude instructions or tell it to stop by commenting @claude.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free – how it went

As a final step, Claude Approvals references whatever policy the user or team abides by (which developers provide as a repo file), and additional signals developers set, like Code Review findings, before approving changes autonomously if allowed. If not, it will seek out “deeper human sign-off,” Anthropic said.

“It works like a smarter CODEOWNERS file,” the release added. Anthropic said it recommends that most customers enable those additional checks “first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals’ green light.”

Admins can select which repos the feature runs in and adjust settings as needed.

But Claude Ship isn’t meant for everyone.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” Anthropic said in the release, noting that its own Claude Code team uses Claude to write a majority of the code it needs.

ZDNET senior contributing editor David Gewirtz said the idea of shipping code at the speed of writing it “raises the hair on the back of my neck.” But he added that, given how impressive Claude Code has been thus far, he wouldn’t be surprised if Anthropic’s deployment tools were equally effective.

Also: Claude Code vs. Codex: Why I use both and how to choose one (if you must)

“But, it does depend on the team’s workflow and the kind of development they’re doing,” he said. “It’s not something for every team and certainly not for every indy developer, but for certain deployment processes, it could shave a ton of time off turnaround, saving money and potentially sending fixes to customers much faster. ‘Tis cool.”

Ultimately, Gewirtz said he has reasons to both trust the tool and be concerned about what it means for younger developers in the workplace.

“Since that workflow is often assigned to less experienced members of the team, it’s likely that Claude would be as accurate, although it’s one more way to shut the junior members out of where they add value to the company and grow their skills to become senior decision makers,” he said.

Developer platforms overall are adapting to the new state of the industry. Entire, a GitHub competitor started by the Microsoft-owned platform’s former CEO, is built around the expectation that developers are working side-by-side with agents.

Individuals with a Pro, Max, or Ultra subscription can use the /ship command now available in Claude Code, meaning “users won’t notice any significant increase in token usage,” an Anthropic representative explained. Team and Enterprise users can use Claude Ship for Github repos, and it is billed on tokens, so your overall bill may change.

Still, that depends on the number of PRs users are putting through Claude Ship — to avoid any surprises, admins can set spending limits for both Code Review and the new PR Steward agent. They can also turn Claude Ship on for an entire repo, meaning developers won’t need the /ship command.

Anthropic added that certain Enterprise organizations “can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits to use within 30 days of claiming” by Jan. 15, 2027.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Say goodbye to accidentally silencing your alarms.

A lesser-known iOS 27 feature includes a new alarm volume setting that gives alarms, timers, and ringtones independent volume control. You can adjust the volume settings for alarms and timers independently of your phone’s alerts and system sounds, so you don’t miss an alarm after lowering your ringtone volume.

Also: Apple reveals daily limits on your Siri AI use – here’s how much you’ll have to pay

There have been ways to adjust the iPhone alarm volume for a few years, but there’s an important distinction between what the new feature entails and what those methods involve.

Previously, you could adjust your Sleep Schedule alarms to always go off at a specific volume, regardless of the iPhone’s shared volume. Sleep Schedule alarms have a dedicated volume slider that you can set and adjust as needed, all configured within the Sleep focus. The new feature, however, lets you set an independent volume for all alarms and timers, not just those in the Sleep Schedule.

Alarms, Timers, Alerts, and System Sounds are set to match your ringtone volume by default, but you can turn them off in the Sounds and Haptics setting.

Also: 5 new Apple Health features you should try in iOS 27.3 – if your phone qualifies

Once you disable the option to match your alarm volume to your ringtone’s volume, you can set your volume for upcoming alarms. With this feature, you can maximize your alarm volume without affecting the volume of incoming calls and notifications.

#2986. Fantastic News for SpaceX Stock Investors!

The FCC just handed SpaceX a first-of-its-kind authorization.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 28, 2026 at 11:01AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.83%) pulled off one of the biggest IPOs in history this year, partly because of the company's aggressive vision and goals, including making space tourism more accessible and building a human colony on Mars. It's hard to see how that's going to be possible anytime soon, but provided SpaceX can achieve some of its ambitions, the company might deliver life-changing returns over the long run. And recently, SpaceX got one step closer to meeting one of its objectives. Here's what investors need to know.

Much of the optimism surrounding SpaceX's future stems from its potential in the artificial intelligence (AI) market. SpaceX argued that it could tap into a $26.5 trillion AI opportunity. That number sounds unrealistic, but the company's recent financial results indicate that its AI business is booming. In the third quarter, SpaceX's revenue increased by 161% year over year to $14.6 billion. The company's Super Intelligence segment posted $7.6 billion in revenue, up 830% compared to the year-ago period.

It accounted for about 52% of SpaceX's top line. Management pointed out that there is soaring demand for compute capacity. And while SpaceX plans to bring more power online, the Earth-bound AI build-out faces various limitations, including limited electricity availability, significant cooling and water requirements, and competition for suitable data center sites. That's why SpaceX wants to send data centers into space, and recently the rocket company received an important regulatory nod in that direction.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission authorized SpaceX to launch up to one million sun-powered orbital data center satellites. It was the first authorization of its kind in U.S. history, and a significant milestone for SpaceX.

SpaceX's regulatory milestone is great news for the company and its shareholders, especially since there was some opposition to this authorization coming from various parties, including Amazon (AMZN +3.96%), among others. These detractors argued that SpaceX's plan could exacerbate orbital debris and congestion, thereby raising the risk of satellite collision. But SpaceX now has its authorization in its back pocket. However, that was just step one.

And as hard as it can sometimes be to obtain the appropriate licenses and authorizations in the space launch industry, this may have been the easiest step of them all. Consider the problem of actually sending these AI satellites into orbit. SpaceX will likely do it on its Starship rocket. Assuming it can carry up to 60 AI satellites per launch, it would take 16,667 launches to deploy the entire constellation. Even if Starship ramps up to a five-launch-per-day cadence, it will take about nine years to complete the job.

But there is significant uncertainty because we aren't sure how many AI satellites Starship can actually carry. Further, Starship is still undergoing test flights, and it may not reach a regular launch cadence for years. But that's not the end of it. Even assuming SpaceX does figure out this problem, there are others. AI satellites in space will face various problems: power supply issues, maintenance, hardware upgrades, and much more. Can SpaceX make this plan commercially viable?

It's not clear, and the company itself has highlighted this potential uncertainty. And we haven't even considered the possibility that demand for AI compute capacity will slow considerably, which could put a real dent in the company's plans. So, even though SpaceX's regulatory authorization to send a million AI satellites into space was a major milestone, this should barely move the needle for investors considering the stock right now.

Meanwhile, the stock remains rather expensive, even after sliding in recent weeks. At 44.1x forward earnings, the market is pricing in years of success. That's why I'd rather stay away from SpaceX for now.

#2985. Fast Fashion Fiasco: Shein to Pay $100 Million in FTC Complaint

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The company agrees to the fine after the FTC alleged it deceived US customers.

Shein, one of the biggest fast-fashion brands in the world, has been ordered to pay $100 million by the Federal Trade Commission, which alleges that the Singapore-based online retail giant engaged in deceptive practices that left millions of US customers dissatisfied with its products and policies.

The FTC complaint alleges that Shein failed to follow through on its swift shipping policies, made it difficult for customers to resolve purchase issues and stifled negative customer reviews from seeing the light of day.

The complaint also alleges problems with the company’s supply chain, false information about the origin of the cotton used in its clothes, a failure to communicate shipping updates to customers and a lack of support for those whose packages were late or went missing altogether.

“The company misled millions of consumers about its products, its suppliers and the authenticity of its customer reviews,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Shein has ballooned over the past decade into the ultra-fast-fashion brand we know today, thanks in large part to the impact influencers have had on social media, posting videos trying on clothing supplied by the company.

In 2026, the company is estimated to ship roughly 1 million packages to US customers daily, according to the FTC. That number becomes even more astounding when you consider that Shein, the FTC alleges, employed just five customer service agents to answer calls from American customers.

This isn’t the first time Shein has faced negative scrutiny. Over the years, the company has faced allegations of numerous workers’ rights violations and is the largest polluter in the fast-fashion industry.

According to Yale Climate Connections, the company emitted 16.7 million total metric tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere in 2023. Comparatively speaking, that’s more than the pollution output of four coal power plants. Shein has since pledged to improve its treatment of workers and reduce carbon emissions, but scrutiny persists.

The $100 million will be used to compensate customers. And according to the FTC’s proposed order, the company, which earned roughly $50 billion in revenue in 2025, will not be able to continue advertising inaccurate shipping and delivery times; negative reviews will no longer be hidden; and its customer service offering will be bolstered.

“The agreement does not constitute an admission of liability, and we continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC’s characterization of our business and compliance practices,” a Shein spokesperson told CNET.

Gemini gave me a little tough love and told me what I needed to hear about my finances.

Google has added Wallet integration to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, letting you learn about your spending habits, plan a budget, maximize credit card rewards, and more with a simple Search.

Starting today, Google announced, Personal Intelligence for Search is expanding to more apps, including Wallet and Drive. Google can’t move or manage any money, but it can give you tailored, personalized search results about your finances, like showing where you spend the most, identifying recurring subscriptions you might not be aware of, and suggesting which credit card might be best to use for travel. All you have to do is ask in a search.

Also: I tried Personal Intelligence in Android Auto – and it knew exactly where I wanted to go

This feature comes just over a week after Google introduced Personal Intelligence to Wallet.

To turn on the feature, go to https://gemini.google.com. Once you’re there, click on the Settings gear icon, and then “Personal Intelligence.” Choose “Connected Apps,” and you’ll see all available apps. When you choose Wallet, you might need to log in to your bank account to access it fully.

Once your Wallet is connected, it takes a few minutes to fully sync. Once it’s finished, you can ask questions through AI mode in Search.

I decided to give it a try for myself, starting off with a simple query: “Based on my spending, what’s a quick way I can save money?” I could have told you one of the primary culprits, but Google happily responded with what I already knew: far too much of my money goes to fast food and coffee.

“You frequently grab quick-service meals,” the response said, pointing out several fast food places that I do indeed frequent, “and specialty coffees throughout the week.” If I just cut that down to two meals and two coffees a week, Gemini explained, I’d save about $30 a week, or $1,500 a year.

Also: This powerful Gemini setting made my AI results way more personal and accurate

When I asked it to find recurring subscriptions, Gemini noted that I had several monthly charges. What I didn’t ask for, but it did, was to break down those subscriptions into an easy-to-see chart, complete with the name, price, category, the card it’s being charged to, and the timeframe it usually comes out. Gemini even offered a few free alternatives to services I was paying for.

Since Gemini also knows what cards are linked to your Wallet, it’s able to offer advice there, too. I’m planning a trip to New York City, so I asked which cards might be best to use for the hotels and airfare. Gemini was able to analyze my card benefits, considering things like rewards and built-in travel insurance, and make a recommendation.

While Gemini Personal Intelligence can access your Gmail to learn more about your spending, it can’t access your bank account. The only information it knows about your finances and spending comes from receipts in your inbox or from your Wallet transaction history. I do use Wallet often (mostly when ordering through online apps), but it’s not quite my go-to option when I’m in a store. Given how useful this feature can be, though, I might just start using Wallet more to give it more information to work with.
