#2961. Eli Lilly vs. Pfizer: Which Healthcare Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Eli Lilly's 45.5% revenue jump and Pfizer's 9.3x forward P/E frame a sharp contrast, with valuation doing much of the talking.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 28, 2026 at 11:42AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Eli Lilly ›

The healthcare landscape is shifting as obesity treatments soar while legacy drugmakers pivot toward new therapeutic areas. Investors must decide between the high-flying growth of Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY +0.01%) and the value-based stability of Pfizer Inc. (PFE +0.21%).

Both companies are giants in the medical world but represent very different investment philosophies. Eli Lilly is currently focused on high-demand metabolic and diabetic treatments, while Pfizer is leveraging its post-pandemic cash reserves to rebuild its portfolio through large-scale acquisitions and oncology research.

Eli Lilly is a global pharmaceutical leader that discovers and markets medicines across approximately 90 countries. The company has a diverse portfolio, but it is currently defined by its dominance in the metabolic space among pharmaceutical stocks. It manages U.S. distribution through major wholesalers including McKesson Corp. (MCK -0.15%), Cencora Corp. (COR +0.08%), and Cardinal Health Inc. (CAH -0.02%).

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $86.5 billion, representing growth of approximately 45.5% compared to the prior period. This expansion supported a GAAP net income of $27.6 billion during those same 12 months. The significant increase in both top- and bottom-line figures highlights the strong demand for the company's newest therapeutic offerings.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 1.6x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity to show how much a company relies on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term debts with short-term assets, is 1.6x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was $9.0 billion.

Pfizer is a research-based biopharmaceutical company that supplies vaccines and medicines to approximately 200 countries and territories. The company is currently focused on expanding its oncology and metabolic portfolios to offset the decline in pandemic-related product sales. Recent strategic moves include the acquisition of Seagen and Metsera to bolster its long-term drug pipeline.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 27, 2026, revenue reached $63.6 billion, reflecting growth of around 1.3%. The company reported GAAP net income of $4.0 billion during this period as it worked through various integration and restructuring costs. This level of revenue shows the company is finding a new baseline after several years of volatile vaccine demand.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.8x, indicating a conservative use of leverage relative to its equity. The current ratio is 1.2x, suggesting the company maintains enough liquid assets to cover its upcoming obligations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was $9.1 billion, providing ample capital for dividends and further research.

Eli Lilly faces risks associated with high research and development failure rates and the extreme costs of bringing new drugs to market. Intense global competition from generic manufacturers and potential government-mandated price controls from the Inflation Reduction Act could pressure its future net margin. Additionally, the company relies on third-party suppliers and raw materials from China, making it vulnerable to supply chain disruptions.

Pfizer faces the challenge of revenue concentration in a few key products that may soon lose patent protection to biosimilar competitors. The company is also navigating the high integration costs and execution risks associated with major acquisitions such as Seagen and Metsera. Furthermore, legal risks remain a factor, including product liability claims and ongoing challenges to the validity of its existing patents.

Pfizer appears to be the more conservative choice for value-seeking investors due to its lower Forward P/E and P/S ratio.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Eli Lilly & Co. is perhaps the fastest-growing large cap pharmaceutical stock around, with a massive sales jump last year. Lilly is riding a wave of success with its GLP-1 drugs Zepbound for weight loss and Mounjaro for diabetes control. There is still plenty of growth left in the treatment, and that is expected to power revenue up more than a third in 2026, to $91.7 billion, with close to $31 billion in net income.

Its next weight-loss drug, Retatrutide, is hotly anticipated for its triple-agonist approach, which is expected to exceed the weight-loss results of Zepbound. The company is also targeting less affluent customers with a lower-cost GLP pill called Foundayo, which it sells directly to consumers.

Besides GLP-1s, Lilly is working on a small interfering RNA therapeutic targeting lipoprotein(a) for the prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in patients with elevated lipoprotein(a) levels. Analysts believe it will be a blockbuster ($1 billion or more in lifetime revenue) if approved.

Meanwhile, Pfizer isn't a hot growth stock, but it's also one of the giants of the pharmaceutical industry.

The company had a post-COVID-19 letdown of sorts, as pandemic-related demand ebbed, but the business has been flexing its might this year. In its first quarter of this year, Pfizer beat Wall Street analysts' expectations on sales and net income. That is partly because Pfizer has been buying growth, having recently acquired oncology specialist Seagen and posted 20% growth in that business's products.

Pfizer is also allocating significant resources to new drug development, with 20 drug development starts scheduled for 2026 and eight data readouts expected, which report on the progress of treatments in development. After falling behind in the GLP-1 weight-loss drug market, Pfizer is also making strides toward becoming a competitor, with very positive Phase II (of III) trial results for an injectable GLP-1 reported earlier this year.

For the current fiscal year, Pfizer revenue is seen slumping slightly to $62.2 billion, while net income is seen rising $1.2 billion to $8.9 billion

Even though Pfizer is priced as a bargain and Lilly shares come at a premium, Long-term investors should be willing to pay up for Eli Lilly and enjoy the many years of growth ahead.

#2960. These Galaxy Z Fold 8 Tweaks Will Help You Take Full Advantage of Its 2 Screens

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 has a refreshing new design for a foldable phone, but you need to change these settings to make the most of it.

I’ve used and reviewed at least a dozen phones this year, but I keep coming back to the Galaxy Z Fold 8. This foldable phone brings me a strange sense of joy that hasn’t diminished even a few months after its launch (and despite the arrival of a popular rival). I like its symmetrical, thin and lightweight design, but it’s the customizable software experience that’s kept me hooked.

Out of the box, the Galaxy Z Fold 8, like other phones, is quite rigid software-wise. The home screen layout on the cover display is locked to a four-column grid, its camera settings aren’t configured to maximize their potential and you might not know about the multitasking improvements.

Thankfully, you can change these settings, but you’ll need to dive into a few additional tools beyond just the standard Settings menu to do so.

I spent two hours setting up my new Samsung foldable. The process involved installing a couple of apps, changing a few settings and adding new Good Lock plugins. If you’re buying a Galaxy Z Fold 8 this holiday season or have had it for a while, I recommend these changes for a finer, more reliable and personalized experience.

Good Lock is a Samsung app made for Galaxy phones. You can download it through the Galaxy Store. It’s the first app I install on a Samsung flagship device because it offers customization options that aren’t available by default. For the Galaxy Z Fold 8, I want to highlight two plugins: Home Up and One Hand Operation Plus.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8’s cover screen doesn’t allow a five-column grid and wastes a lot of space on the home screen. You can’t go past the four-column layout, even if you reduce the icon size (its default icon size is too large for my liking).

If you want a more efficient use of this space, I recommend downloading the Home Up plugin through the Good Lock app (you can easily locate it under the Plugins tab). It lets you change this layout and place icons anywhere you want. You can add up to seven apps in a row or column for a 7-by-7 layout.

I installed it so I could place all my most-used apps and folders on the right side of the home screen for easy one-tap access. I can reach these apps without readjusting my grip. The layout also looks cleaner and more organized. You can perform similar changes to the app drawer by going to the Good Lock app > Home Up > Home screen > Apps list cover column.

One-hand use is my top priority, and the Fold 8’s wide design isn’t the most ergonomic for system UI elements located on the left side or at the top of the screen. For example, when I need to pull down the Quick Settings Panel, I have to swipe down from the top (I’ve set the pull-down gesture on the home screen to open the Notifications panel). I don’t like readjusting my grip every time I need to adjust a “quick” setting. That’s why I installed One Hand Operation Plus and recommend you do the same.

This Good Lock plugin allows you to add gesture handles to the left and right sides of the screen. You can even reprogram Android’s default swipe back gesture. One Hand Operation Plus lets you add up to six shortcuts within the Short swipe and Long swipe gestures. You can choose from Straight, Diagonal up and Diagonal down swipes.

For my use, I have set the diagonal swipe down from the right side to open the Quick Settings panel. This is a minor change that you’ll appreciate in the long run. Day in and day out, when I need to access Quick Settings, it is no different than swiping down on the home screen to access the Notifications panel. I’ve also set a diagonal swipe up to open the Calculator app because I use it often.

You can also add more functionality with a Long swipe gesture. For instance, a Diagonal down swipe could open the Quick Settings panel, while a long Diagonal down swipe could open a specific setting or app. Samsung also lets you fine-tune the touch area by adjusting the Width, Size and Position.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 cameras aren’t as versatile as the less-expensive Galaxy S26 Ultra’s or the ones found in its more expensive Fold 8 Ultra sibling. It lacks a telephoto lens for optical zoom, so you can’t take sharp photos at 3x or 5x zoom. Instead, the phone’s digital zoom crops into the image captured by the 50-megapixel wide camera. However, you can improve the digital zoom results by changing a few settings within the Camera app.

The Samsung Camera Assistant might be mistaken for a pro feature, but it isn’t. I recommend installing this on every Galaxy flagship phone to get the best output from their camera sensors. To find these hidden settings, you need to go to the Camera app and tap the four-dot menu. Then go to Settings > Camera Assistant > Install.

The very first setting you need to change is the resolution. The Fold 8 has two 50-megapixel cameras but its default resolution is set at 12 megapixels, presumably to save space. I recommend changing it to 24 megapixels for more detailed shots and improved results in 2x as well as 4x zoom. You can do so by going to the Camera settings and then:

While you’re at it, I also recommend adding a 2x zoom shortcut in the viewfinder. Open the Camera Assistant again and turn on the very first setting: 2x crop zoom shortcut.

I often use the 50-megapixel mode, but setting the default resolution to 24 megapixels is the most efficient way to get better-quality photos. It gives you sharper photos with better clarity (at both 1x and 0.6x zoom) without taking up as much storage as the 50-megapixel mode. For the best quality at 4x zoom, I recommend changing the resolution to 50 megapixels so you can get photos like those I embedded from Instagram.

This isn’t an additional app, but something you should be aware of on the Galaxy Z Fold 8. Samsung improved the multitasking experience on its 2026 foldable lineup. The Fold 8 series allows you to use the split-screen mode in a 90:10 split. It comes in handy when I’m typing in a Google Doc but need to keep my research material visible at a glance.

This is much more intuitive than a 50:50 split because I can, at any given moment, expand one app and trigger the on-screen keyboard comfortably without exiting the split-screen mode.

It is also more intuitive to drag and drop apps in a multitasking mode. You need to go to the Recents menu (swipe up and hold on the home screen), tap and hold the app and drop it on either half of the screen or use it as a pop-up app. The Recents menu then remembers your app grouping for easy access. For instance, if I add Chrome and Google Docs to a split-screen layout and then move to watch Reels on Instagram, I can move back to the split-screen mode by simply going to the Recents menu and tapping on the app group.

#2959. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#2958. Tech Stock Sell-Off: Down 13%, Is Amazon a Buy Now?

Amazon's $220 billion AI spending plan looks less risky when you see the cloud business and the $578 billion backlog behind it.

By Patrick Sanders – Nov 28, 2026 at 11:45AM EST

Amazon (AMZN +3.96%) is one of many victims in this past month's sell-off of tech stocks, with shares falling 13% from their all-time high.

Investors seem concerned that big tech companies are spending too much on AI infrastructure right now, and Amazon has certainly been one of the biggest spenders. The e-commerce and cloud computing giant expects capital expenditures of $220 billion this year, much of it going toward data centers and AI infrastructure for Amazon Web Services (AWS).

But unlike some other companies spending heavily on AI, Amazon already has an enormous business generating revenue from those investments. I think the recent sell-off presents an opportunity to buy this Magnificent Seven stock at an attractive price.

AWS is the world's largest cloud infrastructure provider, with approximately 28% of the global market, and business is booming. Third-quarter AWS revenue increased 39% to $46 billion, its fastest growth in nearly five years. AWS also generated $17.8 billion in operating income, accounting for more than 60% of Amazon's total operating profits.

There's plenty of business waiting in the pipeline. AWS reported a whopping $578 billion backlog at the end of the quarter, representing future revenue from customers who have committed to its cloud services.

Amazon is also developing its own AI chips, including Trainium, to reduce its dependence on expensive third-party processors. Demand for its custom chips is growing, and CEO Andy Jassy expects AWS revenue to grow more than 40% annually in both 2027 and 2028.

But Amazon's enormous spending is taking a toll on free cash flow. The company generated $168.3 billion in operating cash flow over the trailing 12 months, but free cash flow fell to negative $42.4 billion, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier.

That's a substantial investment, and Amazon will need to keep growing AWS revenue to justify it.

For all the concerns about AI spending, Amazon's underlying business is performing extremely well. Q3 revenue increased 12% to $201.9 billion, while operating income jumped 61% to $28.1 billion. Amazon's operating margin reached a company record of 13.9%.

That's important because Amazon isn't relying entirely on AI to drive its growth. Its e-commerce operations remain formidable, and AWS is growing thanks to rising demand for cloud computing and AI services.

I don't expect Amazon to slow its AI spending anytime soon. However, with AWS growing at its fastest rate in years and Amazon's retail business becoming more efficient, I think the company is well positioned to benefit from its investments.

Now down 13% from its all-time high, Amazon offers investors an opportunity to buy a highly profitable company with an outstanding cloud computing business. I'm bullish on its long-term prospects, and I'd happily buy the dip.

#2957. What Is a Reconditioning Fee on a Used Car?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Used-car dealers may charge you a reconditioning fee to cover their costs of getting cars ready for sale.

A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car. It’s intended to cover any costs the dealer incurs to make sure a used car is showroom-ready, from mechanical inspections to detailing.

The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:

A visual exterior inspection. An auto tech does a quick walk-around the vehicle and notes any corrosion, damage or wear.

An interior inspection. The engine and auto interior are examined and tested, and any issues are documented.

A test drive. The car is taken out for a drive to check that it runs well and that the radio, brakes, A/C and other components are all functioning properly.

Service and repair. Any interior or exterior mechanical, functional or cosmetic issues that were found are repaired, including paint, dents, oil changes and major engine work.

Inspection. Once repairs are completed, the car is inspected again to make sure everything looks and functions as it should.

Detailing. This includes deep interior, engine and exterior cleaning as well as any necessary leather refurbishing, bumper repair or wheel restoration.

Reconditioning fees are legal, but that doesn’t mean you have to pay them. Dealers can charge whatever they want for a reconditioning fee, and it’s not uncommon to find them ranging from around $500 to over $2,000.

The good news: Reconditioning fees, like most dealer extras, can be negotiable. Ask the dealer for a breakdown of the reconditioning fee to see what kind of work was done to prepare the car for sale. If the work was minor but the fee is high — for example, if they’re asking for $1,995 but replaced the floor mats only — that’s a good sign it’s a bogus charge.

However, when it comes time for negotiation, don’t just haggle over the reconditioning fee or other individual fees. The best way to negotiate is to focus on the out-the-door price, or the total amount you’re paying for the car. This simplifies the negotiation process and keeps you focused on the true price of your car.

All dealers invest some amount in reconditioning, but those costs are often built into the dealer’s asking price for a vehicle, rather than as a separate charge.

Some dealers opt to add a reconditioning fee to the bill because it allows them to advertise a lower asking price online, which doesn’t include fees. It’s a tactic to get you into their dealership, since the asking price is lower than that of other dealerships.

However, once you arrive, you may find that the out-the-door price is the same — or more — compared with what other dealers are asking.

Some car-buying experts recommend avoiding dealerships that charge reconditioning fees altogether. But remember that the out-the-door price is what matters at the end of the day, so it’s worth comparing prices at multiple dealerships to find the best deal.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like car buying, so we sifted through Reddit threads to get a sense of how users feel about reconditioning fees. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

Reddit users are generally skeptical toward reconditioning fees. Many users view these fees as a bait-and-switch tactic: dealers advertise an attractive price online and then tack on the fee at the dealership, inflating the actual out-the-door cost well above what was listed. Car buyers frequently share stories of being hit with reconditioning fees ranging from a few hundred dollars up to $2,000 or more, often with little or no evidence of what work was actually done.

Car-buying experts on Reddit point out that most dealerships already build reconditioning costs into the sticker price, so if the fee is listed separately, the dealership may be double-dipping. Several users suggest that car buyers ask their dealer for an itemized breakdown of the work done, but most users recommend negotiating the total out-the-door price rather than individual fees.

#2956. Spelling Out Intrinsic Value Using the Alphabet

The team tackles the complicated and nuanced topic of intrinsic value, the “logical” valuation equalizer championed by famed investor Warren Buffett.

By Motley Fool Staff – Nov 28, 2026 at 12:00PM EST

In this episode of Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing, Motley Fool contributors Jon Quast, Matt Frankel, and Rachel Warren discuss:

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

This podcast was recorded on Nov. 16, 2026.

Jon Quast: Spelling out intrinsic value using the Alphabet, Motley Fool Hidden Gems investing starts now. Welcome to Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing. I'm your host today, Jon Quast, and I am joined by foolish contributors Rachel Warren and Matt Frankel. On today's episode, we're going to go to the Mailbag, and we're also going to let our guest pitch a stock each to you, our listeners. But first, I want to talk about intrinsic value. On last week's episode, we did briefly touch on this concept of intrinsic value. We teased maybe doing a full episode on it, and that was well received by you, so thank you for that. We're going to dive into that here today, talking about intrinsic value. Now, last week, we did touch on the subject because we were talking about Berkshire Hathaway. Longtime Berkshire Hathaway CEO Warren Buffett was a person who really championed this concept of intrinsic value. One of the things that he talked about was it's the only logical way to compare businesses. If you are a value-minded investor, you know that sometimes we use different metrics for different classes of companies. We're going to value a bank one way, an insurance company one way, but maybe we're going to value a tech company another way. Intrinsic value is this great equalizer here. It's really important, and that's why I'm going to kick it off here to Rachel First to just kind of walk us through from a theoretical dictionary way, what is intrinsic value?

Rachel Warren: When we talk about intrinsic value, we're basically asking a simple question. What is this business actually worth based on the cash it can generate over its entire lifespan, adjusted for time and risk? That's very different from book value. Book value is more of an accounting snapshot of what a company owns today versus what it owes on its balance sheet. Book value looks backward at historical costs. Intrinsic value looks forward at future earning power rather than just counting yesterday's assets. You could give a concrete example for this. Imagine you buy a local laundromat or a rental property. You wouldn't just look at the price of the washing machines and the laundromat; for example, you'd look at how much cash is leftover in your pocket every year after paying the water bill, after you pay the taxes, after you make repairs, and then you would decide how much you're willing to pay today for that stream of future cash.

So with a public stock, intrinsic value works in a similar way. Investors estimate the free cash flow a company will produce year after year, and then discount those future dollars back to what they're worth today. Because a dollar 10 years from now is worth less than a dollar in your hand today. Inflation, risk is part of the reason for that. Then when you add up the discounted cash flows and divide by the number of shares, you get an estimate of intrinsic value per share.

Jon Quast: Matt, is there anything that you would add to that definition?

Matt Frankel: No, I mean, that's a good thing, but I would say, be careful when you look at book value and how you incorporate it into intrinsic value, because for different industries, especially, there's a lot of accounting issues. Book value is an accounting number, period. Intrinsic value is what you want to find for the actual value of the company. So that's not a great dictionary definition. But book value, it's an accounting term that like for real estate companies, which is a big area I follow, it tracks the amount that these companies paid for their properties. Now, if you bought an office building 20 years ago, the value of that office building today is not the same thing, but that's what's going to be reflected in your book value. There are really good opportunities, and we can get to this later to find companies that are trading below their intrinsic value and are overlooked because of these accounting issues that might make book value look different than it actually is.

Jon Quast: I hope that our listeners here are able to start understanding why this is such a powerful concept. Essentially, with intrinsic value, you're able to say, Here's what the business is actually worth. If you can figure out what the business is actually worth and lo and behold, the stock price is below that price, then you're able to buy a company objectively for less than it's worth. Now, here's where the rubber meets the road. Warren Buffett saying that he and his long right-hand man, Charlie Munger, would look at the same company, have the same data in front of them, and come up with different numbers of intrinsic value. I think that if I'm an investor, I really want this to be a science. I want to nail this down. I don't like the ambiguity for something that seems like it could be so powerful. Matt, why is this something that is hard to nail down precisely?

Matt Frankel: Well, it's hard to nail down, and I apologize to anyone listening who is expecting a formula for intrinsic value because we can't do that. If you ask five stock analysts what Berkshire Hathaway's intrinsic value is, you're likely to get five different answers. But that's also what can make intrinsic value investors advantage. Because you develop your own way of finding it, you develop your own methods. That's really why intrinsic value is such an important concept. You can make different estimates of your own intrinsic value on your own. You can make a bull case, a bear case, for the same stock.

There are several different textbook methods, the discount cash flow models is one that we could talk about. Where the intrinsic value of a company is based on all of its future cash flows, adjusted for the present value of money. This is going to sound like an Economics 101 lesson and I don't want to put anyone to sleep, so I won't go into that too deep. But there are textbook methods. There are ways. Obviously, like, Buffett doesn't just use the discount cash flow model to the textbook because everyone else would be able to see where there is intrinsic value as well. This is the secret sauce a lot of investors have. Is that they develop their own ways to find intrinsic value, especially intrinsic value that other investors are overlooking. Sorry, I'm not going to give you a formula for intrinsic value. But again, that's also what makes it such a cool part of your investing tool.

Jon Quast: Rachel, I think that people, some investors out there, call foul on this concept because part of the definition of intrinsic value is all the future cash flows that a business can produce. Then you have some companies out there, I think Birkenstock. Isn't that like a 200-year-old company at this point? I mean, we're not going to invest for the lifetime. We're not going to invest for the lifetime of Birkenstock. It's like, Well, I'm going to want to sell this stock someday. I don't want to hold it through the entire lifetime of the company. Where does that fit into? I'm investing today, and maybe I have a 10-5 year horizon, but I'm trying to calculate intrinsic value. How do we reconcile these things as investors?

Rachel Warren: I mean, calculating intrinsic value until you really dive into it, it seems cleaner maybe in a textbook than it is in real life, and that's because of time horizons, the terminal value problem is another piece of that. So when you build a discounted cash flow model, when an analyst is doing this, they're usually forecasting a company's cash flows over the next five or 10 years, and then they slap terminal value on that, which would essentially represent everything the business will earn after that window. Now, the element there to bear in mind is that terminal value often makes about 60%-80% of that calculation. Tweaks to a company's long-term growth rate or discount rate, that can really change your answer wildly. That's one of the reasons why intrinsic value is never a single precise number carved in stone, as Matt was noting, you could get a lot of different answers for a single stock from five very adept analysts. You think of intrinsic value as more of a thoughtful range. It's based on how durable you believe a company's competitive advantage really is.

Matt Frankel: I would add to that that the further out you look when you're trying to calculate intrinsic value, the less accurate your calculation is going to get. Forecasting year 15 of a company's cash flow is like predicting what you're going to be doing 15 years from now. Who knows? The further out your forecast is based, this is why I don't like the terminal value and things like that when I'm doing discounted cash flow models, because especially if your terminal value starts at Year 10 or something like that, it's your own assumptions that the path to the next 10 years are not going to be a straight one. I tend to rely more on near-term calculations for intrinsic value and asset valuations, and net asset value is a big concept that I use. But the further out you look, the less accurate your numbers are going to be so just know that going in.

Jon Quast: I don't think we talk about it enough, but humility is such an important trait in investment. I think one of those things that we just don't talk about enough in investing is this concept of humility. You know, you want to have a degree of confidence when you buy a stock, but at the same time, you have to balance that with a humility because there are a lot of unknowns, and if you don't recognize those things, you're going to have a really hard time as an investor. This is all great. Listeners, we're going to keep driving this home with a question from the mailbag here in the next segment. You're listening to Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing.

Welcome back to Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing. So we're going to take a question from our mailbag here from John in Denver. I'm going to shorten it a little bit. How do you guys think about companies that have valuations that get out over their skis? Do you trim them or sell a decent size of your position or just ride the wave? Would really appreciate Matt's advice, if possible. Matt, I am going to throw you here in just a moment, but I just want to touch on the two companies mentioned by John, Ouster. This is a stock that traded at around two times sales three years ago. It shot up nearly to almost 20 times sales earlier this year. That's a 10 times increase in valuation. Traded at about four times sales earlier at the start this year, and then jumped up to 28 times by middle of the year. So a seven times increase in just a matter of months. So, yes, the valuations ran for these two stocks. I appreciate John's question here.

Matt Frankel: So first of all, what a great problem to have. I wish my biggest problem in my portfolio was, Hey, the stock 10Xed, what do I do with it now? But on a serious note, for me, it's a case-by-case basis, and I generally think about it through a framework of four questions. So No. 1, is my investment thesis still intact? Is the stock doing exactly what I want it do? Because I made the mistake of selling Tesla way too early, even though it was doing exactly what I want to do because of valuation concerns. Valuation by itself is a weak reason to sell. So Number 1, is your investment thesis intact? Is the company doing exactly what you want to do? No. 2, how big is your position? This is normally the deciding factor of whether I trim a position that has gone a little too valuation heavy. If a stock makes up 10% of my position, it's usually a bigger case in my mind that I would like to trim, relative to a stock that makes up, say, 2% of my portfolio. Being able to sleep at night is worth more than, the thought of a little bit more gains. So trimming definitely makes sense if the positions a little too large for comfort. Number 3, would I buy the stock if it were at today's price? If I didn't already own it and it was on my radar and it was trading at the price it is now, would I buy shares? That's usually a really good way to determine whether or not you should sell, trim, hold, or buy more. Number 4, and this is a consideration that often gets overlooked, what is trimming the position going to do to your tax bill? If a stock has 10Xed in a taxable account, this is something you really need to take into consideration before making a decision to trim, even if you say 25% of your position, if the stock's 10Xed, that could give you a little tax hit that you're not expecting. So those are the four ways I think about it. But that's all to say, it's a case-by-case basis, so hopefully that little framework helps.

Jon Quast: I appreciate. John is an extreme case here of yes, essentially 10Xing in a short amount of time. #2955. Broadcom vs. Intel: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Broadcom's networking dominance and Intel's costly foundry pivot pull in opposite directions, and the numbers behind each make the choice sharper than it looks.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 28, 2026 at 12:12PM EST

Choosing between Broadcom (AVGO +3.82%) and Intel (INTC +5.38%) requires understanding two very different corporate strategies. One relies on high-margin connectivity leadership, while the other is undergoing a high-stakes structural transformation.

Broadcom focuses on high-end networking hardware and strategic software acquisitions to serve large enterprise customers. Intel is attempting to reinvent itself as a world-class chip manufacturer and designer. This comparison highlights the contrast between established dominance and a complex turnaround effort.

Broadcom sells networking hardware, wireless connectivity chips, and infrastructure software to hyperscalers and system integrators within the semiconductor stocks category. In its latest annual report, the company noted that large electronic component distributors accounted for approximately 48% of net revenue. Aggregate sales to the top five end customers accounted for approximately 40% of net revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 2, 2026, revenue reached $89.1 billion, representing about 48.7% growth compared to the prior period. Broadcom reported GAAP net income for this time frame of approximately $38.3 billion. This financial performance is supported by strong demand for high-speed networking components and the successful integration of large software business units.

As of its November 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is about 0.8x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity, providing a measure of how a company is financing its growth. In the fiscal year ended Nov. 2, 2025, free cash flow reached around $26.9 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 27.5% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, is about 1.7x.

Intel designs and manufactures computing processors, accelerators, and software for the PC, cloud, and enterprise markets. A significant portion of revenue is concentrated in a limited number of customers, with the three largest accounting for about 43% of net revenue in its latest annual report. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business. The company is currently investing heavily to establish its foundry services, which will manufacture chips for third-party designers.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached $59.9 billion, showing approximately 12.1% growth. The company reported a GAAP net loss of about $12.0 billion for this period. This loss reflects the high costs of building out new manufacturing facilities and shifting demand in the broader computing market. Intel is working to regain its position in advanced processing nodes to improve its competitive standing.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 2.0x. This metric indicates a company's ability to meet short-term obligations with its current assets. The debt-to-equity ratio is about 0.4x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, free cash flow was a negative $4.9 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 25.1% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation because SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Broadcom faces significant risks from customer concentration, with a small number of customers accounting for a majority of revenue. The company is exposed to intense competition in the semiconductor and software industries, including from customers that develop their own competing products. Geopolitical tensions, particularly between the U.S. and China, present risks to global supply chains and international operations. Broadcom also relies on a limited number of contract manufacturers, such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., which introduces vulnerability to capacity constraints and price increases.

Intel faces intense competition in the semiconductor industry from companies like Nvidia Corp. (NVDA +0.80%), Qualcomm (QCOM +6.29%), and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +4.56%), as well as hyperscalers developing in-house designs. The strategy to establish its foundry as a major business carries execution risks, including challenges in securing external customers and high capital intensity. Geopolitical instability impacting manufacturing facilities in Israel and supply chains in Taiwan poses material risks. Furthermore, Intel is currently facing multiple class action securities lawsuits related to alleged misrepresentations concerning its PC business.

Broadcom trades at a lower multiple of Forward P/E, which compares stock price to future earnings estimates, while Intel has a lower P/S ratio, measuring market cap against sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Broadcom is seeing tremendous top-line momentum, with management projecting that fiscal 2026 will bring in about $115 billion in sales, almost double 2025's, and that the following year, fiscal 2027, will see revenue double 2026's to $230 billion. Net income in 2026 will be just about twice that of 2025, at $45 billion, with profit of about $79 billion in 2027.

The strength is coming from AI, with its six main hyperscale customers all increasing their long-term orders for chips and other equipment from Broadcom. These six hyperscalers include Alphabet Inc. (GOOG +0.54%), Meta Platforms (META +3.13%) Anthropic (ANT +10.98%), OpenAI and two firms whose names are not disclosed.

There is some risk to all this growth: one is that the AI boom could go bust, but probably more significant is that Broadcom and private equity giant Blackstone (BX +2.53%) have a joint financing venture that finances frontier AI labs to buy Broadcom equipment. The failure of a client to repay the loan or shifts in interest rates could cause problems with the finance arm and the business at large.

Intel is pressing on with its plan to revive its business. In the spring it announced a partnership with Space Exploration Technologies Inc. (SPCX +4.83%) and Tesla Inc. (TSLA +5.22%) to build Terafab, a massive AI chip-making plant aiming to produce as many as 200 billion AI chips a year. Intel is providing its foundry expertise and its 14A process, an effort to produce 1.4-nanometer chips it announced two years ago and is still developing.

Also this year, Intel signed a deal with Nvidia to help build a new AI GPU called Crescent Island that can work in tandem with Nvidia's Blackwell AI chips, and agreed to help develop an AI-centric chip for Google, too. Last year, the company raised investments from the U.S. government and SoftBank to improve its capital position.

All that has generated some optimism on Wall Street. For fiscal 2026, sales are seen rising 17% to $61.7 billion, though a large $11 billion net loss is projected, reflecting the cost of expanding its U.S. foundries.

Broadcom's combination of top-line growth and profitability comes with shares that are remarkably reasonable in terms of forward P/E ratio. When choosing between these two chip makers, go with Broadcom for 2027.

Uncertainty in the Middle East, elevated Treasury yields and fears about an AI bubble continue to keep global markets on edge. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking stable income can consider enhancing their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Chord Energy is an independent exploration and production company with long-lived assets primarily in the Williston Basin. With a quarterly base dividend of $1.30 per share, CHRD offers a dividend yield of 3.67%.

In a research note on third-quarter expectations, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold reiterated a buy rating on CHRD stock with a price target of $175. "We model production near the top of guidance and continue to see strong performance from new wells and base production," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst expects Q3 2026 production at 283 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, or Mboe/d, in line with the Street's consensus and near the high end of the 278 to 284 Mboe/d guidance. Hanold said his Q3 2026 earnings per share estimate increased to $5.29 due to lower non-cash depreciation, depletion and amortization.

Meanwhile, cash flow per share estimate moved lower to $13.59 to reflect Hanold's update based on the current backdrop and commodity mark-to-market. He expects Chord Energy to report capital spending of $375 million for Q3 2026, slightly above the Street's estimate of $369 million.

Overall, Hanold remains bullish on CHRD, given its best-in-class balance sheet. He expects a free cash flow payout of 80% in the third quarter, with the possibility of an upside. Hanold expects investors to focus on management commentary on 2027 capital plans, Williston M&A opportunities, and long-term performance of 4-mile wells.

Hanold ranks No. 310 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Chord Energy KPIs on TipRanks.

Williams, an energy infrastructure company that delivers natural gas, is the next dividend pick. The company recently completed the $5.5 billion acquisition of Momentum Midstream, which will expand its natural gas infrastructure in the Haynesville to meet growing Gulf Coast LNG, power and industrial demand. At a quarterly dividend of $0.5250 per share, Williams offers a yield of 2.89%.

In her latest research note, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $87. Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, the analyst said that she expects WMB to announce strong quarterly performance.

Scotto raised her estimates to reflect insights from the quarterly catch-up call, the completion of the Momentum Midstream acquisition, and mark-to-market quarter-to-date commodity prices. She expects WMB to report Q3 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2,036 million, which is modestly above the Street's consensus estimate.

Furthermore, Scotto expects Williams' Transmission, Power & Gulf segment to increase quarter-over-quarter, driven by the startup of the Socrates power project and favorable natural gas liquids, or NGL, margins.

#2953. What Are Repositioning Cruises?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Repositioning cruises move ships between seasonal destinations, often with longer sailings, fewer port stops and lower fares.

A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another. For example, many ships sail in the Mediterranean Sea during the summer and move to the Caribbean Sea for the winter, and that trip between the two is a repositioning cruise.

Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.

Because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea. For some travelers, that’s a chance to relax and enjoy the ship’s onboard amenities. Sometimes, these sailings can also be cheaper than traditional cruises.

One key consideration for a repositioning cruise is that the embarkation and disembarkation ports will be different. This means you generally can’t buy a standard round-trip flight to and from the same city. Instead, you’ll need transportation to where the cruise starts and another way home from where it ends, which usually means two one-way flights (or one open-jaw ticket) unless you live near one of the ports. While these one-way sailings may be more affordable than traditional cruises, airfare costs may be higher.

This could be a great opportunity to redeem miles for your flight.

Another feature that sets these cruises apart is that stops along the way tend to include ports that aren’t traditionally part of regular itineraries. These might include islands like Bermuda, the Azores or the Canary Islands, and on some northern routes, Greenland.

Just keep in mind that the main purpose of these sailings is to get to a new region for the next season’s itineraries rather than make daily port stops. So if you’re someone who wants to visit as many places as possible on a cruise, a repositioning sailing may not be the ideal choice.

Repositioning cruises are often longer than standard cruises, commonly running two to three weeks compared with about a week for a typical sailing, which may appeal to travelers looking for an extended vacation. The experience is often more relaxed, with many days at sea and less of a rush to book shore excursions or visit important sites when off the ship.

If there are particular ships with certain amenities — like tattoo parlors or massive waterparks — that you really want to experience, keep in mind that not all ships reposition between regions. Some stay in certain regions year-round.

For ships that do change locations for the season, there are plenty of onboard activities to fill the time. You can enjoy shows, food and wine tastings, organized activities and time at the spa, pool or casino.

Many repositioning crossings are relatively smooth, and modern ships use stabilizers to reduce movement. But since these itineraries cross open ocean rather than staying closer to land, there can be more motion, especially on North Atlantic crossings in fall and winter.

If you tend to get seasick, this could be a dealbreaker. Even if a repositioning sailing is smooth, temperatures can be chilly on the open ocean, especially on northerly or spring and fall transatlantic routes, with strong winds that may make suntanning by the pool less appealing.

You can book one of these sailings in the same way you would book a traditional cruise. But if you’re searching for dates and itineraries on a cruise line’s website, they may be listed as transatlantic, transpacific or Panama Canal sailings rather than repositioning cruises, though some lines do use the term "repositioning." There’s even a website that specializes in rounding up these cruises: RepoCruises.com.

Keep an eye out for themed sailings that focus on topics like wine, theater or music, where fellow guests on the ship may share similar interests. Cruise lines often schedule them on repositioning cruises to spur demand.

Here are some repositioning cruises for 2027. They often take place during shoulder seasons, between the most popular cruising times in places like the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

This journey repositions the ship from Miami, where it sails on Caribbean itineraries, to Seattle, where it will visit ports in Alaska during the spring and summer months. Departing April 8, 2027, the 18-night cruise includes stops at various ports in Colombia, Panama and Mexico, as well as San Diego and Los Angeles, before arriving in Seattle on April 26.

Regent Seven Seas Cruises' all-suite luxury ship Seven Seas Mariner will sail between New York and Lisbon, making stops in Canada, Morocco and the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

Departing April 29, 2027, the 16-night journey ends in Lisbon, Portugal, as the ship repositions to Europe, where it will sail various itineraries, including Mediterranean sailings later in the summer season.

Departing Seattle on Sept. 28, 2027, Norwegian Jade will sail to Yokohama, Japan, with stops in Alaska and northern Japan. This is a way to travel across the Pacific with less jet lag, since the journey takes place over several days, with ship clocks typically adjusted gradually (often an hour at a time) during the sailing. Note that the voyage also crosses the International Date Line.

If Greenland has been on your bucket list, this 16-night sailing is a way to get up close and personal with its natural scenery. Departing Reykjavik on Aug. 25, 2027, Azamara Quest will sail from Iceland to the U.S. It will make stops in Greenland, Canada and New England before reaching the Big Apple.

Departing Bergen, Norway, on June 11, 2027, this 28-night sailing aboard Viking Vela sails around Iceland's coast, makes two stops in Greenland and crosses the Atlantic before reaching New York.

#2952. 4 ETFs I'm Holding for the Next 20 Years -- Even If the Market Crashes

Ignore the short-term noise and build your portfolio for the long term.

By David Dierking – Nov 28, 2026 at 12:15PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF ›

A lot of investors spend their energy worrying about what the market will do next. Not as many spend time thinking about what they should do next.

A recent Morningstar study found that the average dollar invested in U.S. equity funds earned 8.7% annually over the past 10 years, while the funds themselves earned 9.9% per year. That's a 1.2% annual drag largely attributed to poorly timed trading. Funds with higher volatility experienced larger-than-average performance gaps.

That's why I tend to focus on finding some of the best long-term buy-and-hold options available. Here are four such exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that I think are ideal for holding over the next two decades, regardless of what the market does.

If you've read any of my advice in the past, you know the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI +1.75%) is my core equity ETF of choice. A lot of people choose the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +1.66%) for this purpose, but I prefer the addition of mid-cap and small-cap stocks to the mix. They only account for about 12% of the fund's total market cap, but they add diversification and higher return potential without significantly altering the core exposure.

As a core portfolio holding, it makes sense to hold this pretty much your entire life in some allocation. Owning large-cap U.S. companies that are durable, generate lots of cash, and have historically weathered every economic environment there's been is the perfect way to build long-term wealth.

The Vanguard Mid-Cap Growth ETF (VOT +1.89%) has a couple of things going for it right now. First, it targets the growth theme, which generally provides better long-term return potential, especially over the course of 20+ years. Second, it diversifies away from mega-cap growth stocks that have led for years. The Vanguard Mid-Cap Growth ETF offers a potentially better entry point for growth stocks.

This fund probably isn't one that you want to weight too heavily in your portfolio. But it's definitely worth considering if you want to lower your exposure to tech (it has only a 20% allocation to this sector) or find something more reasonably valued.

Long-term investments don't need to tilt toward growth. A fund like the iShares MSCI USA Minimum Volatility Factor ETF (USMV +0.98%) can provide the value that eventually leads to outperformance. This ETF doesn't necessarily target low-volatility stocks exclusively. Instead, it starts with a broad universe of stocks and creates the portfolio optimized for minimum overall volatility.

It's worth mentioning that tech is the fund's largest sector holding, so you're not avoiding this risk altogether. But as a holding for the next two decades, the iShares MSCI USA Minimum Volatility Factor ETF provides one of the best opportunities for value without entirely sacrificing growth potential.

Bonds won't be the most exciting part of your portfolio. However, after the Fed's big rate hiking cycle in 2022 and the fact that long-term yields still aren't far from multi-decade highs, they look much more attractive as a long-term opportunity than they have in a while.

The iShares Core Universal USD Bond ETF (IUSB -0.30%) is a great choice for two reasons: It has a slightly higher allocation to corporate bonds (instead of government bonds) than many of its broad market peers, and it introduces a small exposure to junk bonds.

The iShares Core Universal USD Bond ETF is one of the most complete U.S. bond market ETFs around. The 5.2% yield is compelling again, and the balance it provides for equities in a portfolio makes sense for long holding periods.

There are other asset classes you could consider adding to this group, like gold or international stocks. But if you want to create a simple ETF portfolio that's built for the long term, whatever the future holds, these four funds will work great.

#2951. CoreWeave Is Down 40% This Year. Is This a Once-in-a-Lifetime Buying Opportunity?

It depends on whether you think the company’s massive spending is worth it.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 28, 2026 at 12:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than CoreWeave ›

The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution is in full swing. Yet, some notable companies in the industry aren't convincing investors. One of them is CoreWeave (CRWV +3.71%), a corporation that offers cloud-based AI compute capacity through a network of data centers. CoreWeave went public last year in what was a successful IPO. However, the company's shares have dropped 40% this year and are now near the IPO price of $40. Is this an amazing buying opportunity for patient investors focused on the long game?

CoreWeave isn't a particularly big player in the vast cloud computing market. However, demand for the company's services has been soaring. Since it specializes in providing the computing infrastructure needed to train, deploy, and run AI models, and companies are racing to do just that, CoreWeave's business is booming, and that's being reflected in its financial results.

In the third quarter, the company's revenue increased by 168% year over year to $3.7 billion. CoreWeave's year-over-year revenue growth had been slowing sequentially since the tech company went public, before reaccelerating sharply this quarter.

CRWV Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts

That's a great sign for the business. Meanwhile, the company's operating income of $207 million was much higher than the $52 million reported in the year-ago period. However, CoreWeave is spending quite a bit of money to build the infrastructure necessary to support the demand for its services, and then some. That's why the net loss widened during the third quarter, coming in at $709 million -- or $1.27 per share -- versus the net loss of $110 million ($0.22 per share) reported in the prior-year quarter.

CoreWeave also announced that it is raising its capital expenditure guidance for the fiscal year 2026. It now expects it to come in between $37 billion and $39 billion, compared to its previous range of $35 billion to $39 billion. CoreWeave is incurring significant debt to fund its ambitions. It has secured more than $30 billion in debt and equity capital this year.

It currently has about $66.2 billion in debt (including leases, as of the end of the third quarter), which seems like a lot for a company worth $23.67 billion. True, CoreWeave continues to see sustained demand for its services, and this demand may persist for a while. Michael Intrator, CoreWeave's CEO, said demand for infrastructure is outpacing the capacity to deliver it.

That's why CoreWeave is largely sold out through 2027. We can also see this through the company's revenue backlog, which hit $132.5 billion as of the end of the third quarter, representing a 138% year-over-year increase. Now for the interesting part. CoreWeave's debt has ballooned about 457% since the first quarter of 2025, its first update as a public company.

Over the same period, CoreWeave's revenue backlog has grown about 412% -- not as fast as the debt, but the difference isn't huge either. This comparison is meaningful, but it may hide some important details. For instance, CoreWeave is demonstrating meaningful pricing power, having increased its prices across the board this year for various generations of GPUs (graphics processing units).

The company estimates that more than 130,000 GPUs will come off contract next year, with about 170,000 more doing so in 2028. Renewing contracts at current market prices could mean even higher revenue for the company without having to dish out billions to expand its capacity. That means higher margins as well.

That's just one of the dynamics that could lift CoreWeave's revenue and profits over the medium term, but that assumes that the AI tailwind persists. The company also faces a meaningful risk due to significant customer concentration, with just one of its clients accounting for more than 60% of its revenue in fiscal year 2025.

The market has adjusted for these risks, at least somewhat. CoreWeave's current price-to-sales ratio is 2.6, down from 15 in September 2025. That seems like a fair price to me, given CoreWeave's expanding revenue and backlog. Even with rising debt and customer concentration, the stock looks attractive at current levels, though I wouldn't call it a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

Capital optimization tools and disciplined lending are positioning BBVA to convert volume growth into earnings expansion.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 28, 2026 at 12:37PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 29, 2026, BBVA (BBVA +1.62%) announced quarterly net attributable profit of more than 3 billion euros. Strong lending expansion in key markets fuels steady earnings, enabling significant capital returns to shareholders. Three things management said stand out.

Lending activity accelerated across primary geographies, supporting net interest income (NII), the difference between interest earned on loans and interest paid on deposits. Higher loan volumes in key regions now convert directly into profit as interest rate pressures ease.

The Corporate & Investment Banking (CIB) division serves wholesale corporate clients and grows through cross-border trade and corporate lending. Client-driven demand accounts for close to 90% of the division's revenues, reducing reliance on volatile trading operations.

Management uses significant risk transfer (SRT) transactions, regulatory capital relief trades that shift credit risk to third parties, to optimize balance sheet efficiency. These balance sheet management tools free up capital to fund profitable loan expansion and support planned shareholder distributions.

Loan demand across core markets continues to expand, and leadership is showing clear optimism about turning volume into sustainable profit growth. Strong customer acquisition, market share gains in profitable enterprise lending, and low cost-to-income ratios bolster long-term competitive advantages. Executive focus remains centered on pricing discipline and disciplined capital deployment.

Efficiency gains from technology initiatives and risk management tools help sustain profitability metrics. Management expects return on tangible equity (ROTE), a metric that measures profits relative to tangible equity, to remain well above European peers' averages.

#2949. Mortgage Rates Today, Tuesday, November 24: Lower, But …

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates are down this morning, but could seesaw back up tomorrow.

Another day, another substantial swing. This one's lower, but don't count on it starting a trend: We keep seeing mortgage rates move back and forth, but no one's expecting rates to take a dive. If you're watching this space because you're waiting to refinance, it's unlikely your wait is about to end.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.13% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 25 basis points lower than yesterday and unchanged from a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

The amount of day-to-day discrepancy we've been seeing prompted me to take a little cruise around the web this morning to see what 30-year rates lenders are advertising. Mortgage lenders' rates are never identical, but when we're seeing rapid change, the gaps between lenders tend to widen — and that's for sure what I saw. I looked at six different lenders, and saw a nearly 70-basis-point difference between the highest and lowest APRs. (And yes, that was looking for the same loan amount, location and so on.)

My point is, whether you're looking to buy or refinance, make sure to shop multiple lenders. You're the same candidate bringing the same financials to each one, but you could end up with extremely different rate quotes. And it pays to compare. Freddie Mac estimates that comparing at least two lenders could save you up to $600 per year in interest. Compare four or more, and that savings is over $1,200 annually.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context. For more, keep reading below the charts.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Mortgage rates may be lower today, but like I mentioned above, it's been more of a seesaw than a ski slope — and we may be about to hit the high side again. The latest Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index is due out tomorrow morning. Recently, when rates have moved higher, inflation's been in the mix.

Strong inflation's generally bad for borrowing, including to buy a home, because higher interest rates are the remedy. Raising the federal funds rate (the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers of the Federal Reserve actually set) is the Fed's main tactic for managing inflation. While the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, its decisions influence the entire economy. That includes mortgage lenders, who tend to adjust rates ahead of its decisions.

We already know how PCE's likely to go, since it's the last of the three big inflation measures to be released. We've already gotten last month's Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index. October's CPI came in worse than predicted, showing widespread price increases. (When most of the increase is driven by one area, it's easier to be optimistic that inflation can be contained.) And October’s PPI showed wholesale inflation climbed at its fastest pace in almost four years. PPI measures the price businesses pay for things, so it's often a preview of what consumers could face once those costs get passed along.

Predictions for October PCE aren't great, so at this point the hope is that the numbers aren't even worse than expected. And again, PCE's out tomorrow morning. We'll know whether we're getting seconds (actually, thirds) of bad October inflation news well before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Markets are currently anticipating a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December meeting. Even though that'll remain the most likely outcome, a poor showing from PCE could spark speculation about a half-point hike. That probably won't be good for mortgage rates.

But back to the upcoming holiday: Markets will be closed on Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, so we'll all have a bit of a break this week. Mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.63% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#2947. Textron: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Supply chain recovery and military funding clarity are removing the production roadblocks that constrained growth.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 28, 2026 at 12:39PM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 29, 2026, Textron (TXT +1.54%) announced higher full-year profit and cash flow forecasts behind expanding aircraft deliveries. The multi-industry manufacturer relies on pricing discipline and factory automation across its aerospace and defense divisions to offset supply chain bottlenecks. Three things management said stand out.

Customer flight hours remain steady, boosting aftermarket parts revenue and driving commercial turbine and jet sales. Operational investments in assembly automation helped Textron Aviation revenue grow 14% year over year to $1.7 billion.

Congress granted an Above Threshold Reprogramming (ATR) request, which reallocates military budget funds to keep the MV-75 Cheyenne tiltrotor aircraft program funded. That budget move cleared near-term financial hurdles while the defense business scales prototype builds.

Management is divesting its industrial division, which includes golf cart maker Textron Specialized Vehicles and fuel system maker Kautex. Separating these commercial manufacturing units narrows company capital toward pure-play aerospace and defense contracts.

Factory floor parts inventory is back to roughly 2021 levels, easing production constraints on landing gear and engine components. Internal tooling investments and dual-sourcing key parts will support higher output across aircraft lines.

Strategic focus remains on expanding defense contract backlogs and boosting assembly line productivity.
