#2944. Caterpillar vs. Corning: Which Industrials Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Caterpillar's global dealer network and Corning's concentrated customer base pull in opposite directions, and the valuation gap may tip the scale.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 28, 2026 at 12:41PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Caterpillar ›

Caterpillar (CAT +3.32%) and Corning (GLW +4.83%) represent two different ways to play global growth through infrastructure and high-tech materials. Deciding which one to buy for 2027 requires weighing industrial stability against technological innovation.

Caterpillar is a global leader in construction and mining equipment, while Corning specializes in glass and ceramics for smartphones and fiber optics. Comparing them helps you weigh traditional heavy machinery against high-tech components that power the digital age.

Caterpillar operates as a powerhouse in the construction stocks space, providing essential machinery for mining and energy projects. The company relies on a massive global dealer network including 41 independent dealers in the United States and 109 dealers outside the U.S. serving 190 countries. This distribution model enables it to reach original equipment manufacturers and end-users efficiently while maintaining a strong regional footprint through acquisitions such as John Fabick Tractor Company.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $77.8 billion, which represents revenue growth of approximately 20.3%. The company reported GAAP net income of $11.8 billion during this period, reflecting a net margin of 15.2%. This performance follows a trend of increasing revenue as the business navigated demand across its diverse resource and power segments as global infrastructure needs expanded.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 2.0x, meaning total debt is twice the value of shareholder equity. A current ratio of 1.4x measures the ability to pay short-term debts with current assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was $7.5 billion, which represents the cash generated from operations minus capital expenditures.

Corning provides specialized materials science products for everything from emissions control to the glass used in smartphones and tablets. Its sales are highly concentrated, as evidenced by a few key customers accounting for 59% of display sales and 61% of automotive sales. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, making it highly dependent on the success and loyalty of a limited client base.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $17.7 billion, which marks revenue growth of about 18.8%. GAAP net income for the period was $2.1 billion, reflecting a net margin of 12.1% across its various operations. This growth was driven by demand across its optical communications and specialty materials segments as global digital infrastructure and mobile hardware continued to evolve.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.9x, indicating the company carries less debt relative to its equity than its peer. The current ratio stands at 1.6x, showing the business has $1.60 in current assets for every dollar of short-term liabilities. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was $1.4 billion, which represents cash from operations after subtracting capital expenditures.

Caterpillar faces significant risks from cyclical global economic conditions and volatility in commodity prices, which directly impact how much its customers spend on heavy machinery. The company must also manage supply chain disruptions and component shortages, particularly for semiconductors, alongside competition from rivals like Deere & Co. (DE +2.06%) and Komatsu (KMTUF +5.79%). Its financial products segment adds exposure to credit risk and interest rate fluctuations, which could tighten its access to capital.

Corning is vulnerable to manufacturing disruptions because its facilities are geographically concentrated in the Asia Pacific region. The company faces intense competition in the display and optical markets from firms such as Nippon Electric Glass and AGC (ASGLF +0.00%). Furthermore, its heavy reliance on a small group of large customers means that the loss of a single major contract could significantly harm its total revenue and cash flows.

Caterpillar appears more attractively priced with a lower Forward P/E and P/S ratio, which measure future earnings estimates and sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Caterpillar is a classic proxy for the health of the U.S. economy, with business improving when there's more domestic economic activity. Typically, that demand has been for its heavy equipment, but of late, its power and energy business has become the growth engine for Caterpillar, emerging as a strong driver of sales thanks to robust demand for prime and backup power generation in data center markets.

For fiscal 2026, revenue is seen rising 18% to $79.4 billion, with net income rising 38% to $12.3 billion. Growth is expected for 2027, with analyst consensus pegging sales at $88.5 billion and profit at $14.3 billion.

Turning to Corning, recently struck deals with Meta Platforms (META +3.13%), Nvidia Corp. (NVDA +0.80%), and the AWS division of Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +3.96%) have led Corning management to believe it can execute on its so-called Springboard program to jump annual sales to $20 billion this year, $30 billion in 2028, and $40 billion in 2030.

Each deal is in Corning's core areas of expertise: fiber optics and connectivity. These are for AI data centers and new manufacturing plants being planned in the U.S. Much of the new capacity Corning needs to fulfill these deals will come from its own U.S. expansion, reducing its tariff and general geopolitical risk. In its fiscal 2026 third quarter, sales grew 19%, and net income rose about 60% to $660 million. Wall Street consensus sees net income rising 53% to $2.44 billion.

One of the keys to Corning's growth is sharing its development plans with major customers well in advance, allowing it and its partners to tweak plans and development as needed to better meet future needs. The addition of new AI customers also helps reduce its risk of overreliance on Apple Inc. (AAPL +0.83%), which makes the iPhone glass, among other products.

So which is the better buy for 2027? Corning's continual improvement of its fiber-optic and connectivity products has led to impressive growth, with much more on the way. It comes at a premium to Caterpillar, but the business seems on track to deliver management's promised growth.

#2941. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

#2939. How to Get Grants for College

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Grants don’t have to be repaid, but the money can only go toward school-related costs. Here’s how to use grants to pay for school and how to make them go further.

Grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education. It’s free money you aren’t expected to pay back.

Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses. Some grants, depending on who awards them, require an application or have requirements you must meet before you can get your money.

Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.

Federal grants come from the federal government.

State grants come from state programs and often can only be used at schools in that state.

Institutional grants come from your college or university, or even your program or major.

Private grants come from nonprofits, community organizations and individual donors.

To receive a federal grant, you must complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Most states require the FAFSA for state grants, and a few require a separate state application. You’ll need to complete the FAFSA for each year you’re enrolled in school. You may need to meet certain eligibility requirements, such as income limits, to get some grants. The FAFSA is how you apply for the Pell Grant, which is a financial need-based grant. The FAFSA also determines eligibility for federal work-study, which is a job program rather than a grant.

Federal aid, including federal grants, typically requires students to meet satisfactory academic progress. This means you have to maintain a minimum grade point average and be on track to finish your degree on time, as determined by your school. Your school also sets how many credits you must take to qualify for grant funding.

Some grants — typically private or institutional grants — require an additional application that asks for transcripts, letters of recommendation and personal essays. Your school’s financial aid office or the grant provider will have details on applying for specific grants.

After you submit the FAFSA, you’ll receive a financial aid award letter from each school you applied to, which outlines how much in federal, state and institutional grants you’ve been offered. You must accept your aid to receive it.

Most grants will be disbursed directly to your college or university. Your school will apply the grant money first to tuition, fees and any other charges it bills, such as housing or a meal plan.

In some cases, you may receive more grant money than your school bills, which is the best-case scenario. If that happens to you, any leftover funds will likely be refunded to you. Refund timelines vary by school, so it may take some time to get your money. You can get your refund faster by setting up direct deposit with your school. You can then use the funds for other costs approved by your grant — some examples are detailed below.

If you have questions about your grant money, contact your college’s financial aid office.

Grants can help cover cost-of-attendance expenses. Generally, you can use grant money to pay for tuition, textbooks, class materials, transportation, housing and food. Depending on your school’s policies, you can use grant money to cover summer classes or study abroad programs, too.

Some grants come with specific terms about how you can spend them. Check your financial aid award letter or, for a private or institutional grant, the school’s or organization’s website to find specifics.

After your grant is applied to your tuition and school expenses, you can options to fill the gaps between what the grant covers and the total cost of your program. Some options include savings, scholarships, work-study, payment plans, federal student loans or, as a last resort, private loans. By using grants to pay for your college education, you may be able to borrow less.

To maximize the grants you’re eligible to receive, enter accurate information on the FAFSA and complete it as soon as you can — some funds are first-come, first-served. Also, don’t limit yourself to federal or state grants — search and apply for as many privately funded grants as you can find.

Your grant money usually goes straight to your college or university to pay your tuition and fees. Anything that is left over may be disbursed to you for other school-related costs.

Yes, but it depends on your grant. Housing is part of your cost of attendance, so you can use grant money to pay for off-campus rent.

You don’t have to pay back a grant as long as you continue to meet all requirements for the grant, such as staying enrolled. You can use grant money on school and school-related expenses. Some grants may require you to meet eligibility requirements such as a minimum GPA or state residency. If you receive more grant money than your cost of attendance for a given school term, ask your financial aid office if you can put that grant money toward next year’s cost of attendance.

If you have a federal grant like a Pell Grant, these are examples when you may have to repay all or part of the grant:

You received enough scholarship money to reduce your federal aid need.

It depends. You can usually use grant money to buy a laptop. Computers are considered course materials, which fall under cost-of-attendance expenses, so they can be covered by a grant. However, always double-check with the grant provider and your financial aid award letter to ensure that you’re following all restrictions. Whether you can use grant money to cover a laptop depends on your school’s policies and how much grant money you receive.

If you get more grant money than your school bills you, you’ll likely receive the leftover money to spend on other cost-of-attendance expenses. You can use this money on living costs such as transportation or housing. Grant money often goes mostly toward tuition, so a refund isn’t guaranteed.

Grant and scholarship money is generally tax-free when you use it for tuition, required fees, books and required class supplies. If you have additional questions, consider talking to a tax professional.

By Will Healy – Nov 28, 2026 at 12:45PM EST

Walmart (WMT +0.90%) and Costco Wholesale (COST +1.01%) have stood out for beating the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite this year. As most of the stocks in the tech-heavy index have struggled, investors have benefited from the stability offered by these retail giants.

Amid those gains, investors may have forgotten about another venerable retailer outside of the index. Target (TGT -0.14%), which struggled for years amid a series of missteps, has begun to make a comeback under its new CEO, Michael Fiddelke.

Despite Target's considerable returns since Fiddelke took over, it may not be too late to buy. Here’s why.

Admittedly, Target stock has struggled since the end of the pandemic. A less-desired product mix, chronically high inventory levels, and unnecessary political stances that alienated left- and right-leaning shoppers alike were among the challenges that brought about net sales declines.

However, after Fiddelke became CEO on Feb. 1, he announced a $5 billion plan to update stores and supply chains and revamp its product mix. Since he took the job, the company's net sales have stopped falling.

In the first nine months of fiscal 2026 (ended Oct. 31), net sales of $79 billion are up by more than 6% compared to the same period in fiscal 2025. That is a vast improvement from the first three quarters of 2025, when net sales fell by 2% year over year.

Also, despite an 11% increase in selling, general, and administrative expenses, net earnings for the first nine months of fiscal 2026 were $3.9 billion, up 46% from the same year-ago period.

Not surprisingly, these improvements likely helped the stock rise by more than 60% since Fiddelke took over.

Moreover, Target's annual dividend of $4.64 per share has risen for 55 straight years, making it a Dividend King, or a company that has raised its dividend for 50 years or more. While the dividend yield has fallen to 2.7%, it remains well above Walmart's 0.8% dividend return and Costco's 0.5% yield.

Additionally, Target's P/E ratio suggests it is not too late to buy. Despite those increases, Target sells for a fraction of Walmart's valuation. Its price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple is 16, well below Walmart's 50 P/E ratio. Costco is even more expensive, trading at 53 times earnings.

Hence, even with the rising stock price, the tailwinds that have pushed Target stock higher this year appear to remain in place.

Despite Walmart's and Costco's recent successes, Target looks like the better buy.

A series of past missteps weighed on Target's stock, but the company seems to have turned around under new leadership. Amid a reversal of sales declines, its stock price is much higher, and a reasonable valuation suggests it is not too late to buy. When also considering its generous, rising dividend, Target appears to have become an increasingly compelling growth-and-income stock.

Thus, despite Walmart's and Costco's recent gains, Target stock appears to offer the potential for even higher returns.

#2936. 2 Stocks to Buy in the AI Chip Stock Sell-Off and Hold for 5 Years

The sell-off has dragged down two leaders with years of growth still ahead.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 28, 2026 at 1:00PM EST

The market has been volatile in recent weeks, and semiconductor companies have been particularly affected. There are several reasons for that. Here are three of them. First, many investors continue to fear that the artificial intelligence (AI) industry's growth won't last that much longer. With several chip stocks having already gained significantly on the AI tailwind, some are choosing to take profits now. Second, recent scandals surrounding Nvidia's (NVDA +0.80%) CEO, Jensen Huang -- perhaps the most important figure in the industry -- have sent shockwaves through the AI market.

Third, broader macroeconomic and political issues have also weighed on AI stocks, including the recent U.S. midterm elections, in which voters elected many politicians who favor stricter regulation of the AI industry. Despite all that, my view is that the industry has a bright future. And two stocks that could capitalize on it over the next five years are Broadcom (AVGO +3.82%) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +4.56%).

Hyperscalers are increasingly designing their own custom AI chips, which have several advantages. They can be designed to suit the specific computational needs of companies' AI models and workloads, they tend to be cheaper and more energy-efficient than comparable GPUs (graphics processing units), and they help hyperscalers reduce their reliance on Nvidia's hardware. Broadcom is a leader in the custom AI chip market, and it has partnered with several major hyperscalers. Soaring demand for its products is leading to much improved financial results.

In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2026, which ended Aug. 2, Broadcom's revenue increased by 86% year over year to $29.6 billion. The company's AI semiconductor revenue grew 221% year over year to $16.7 billion. Broadcom's non-GAAP earnings per share were $3.32, 96% higher than the year-ago period, while free cash flow came in at $13.7 billion, growing 95% year over year.

While some investors expect the AI tailwind to slow, potentially harming Broadcom's financial results, the opposite may occur. Broadcom has several agreements that run until 2029 (or longer), and it could sign even more as AI spending continues to grow. Consider that Anthropic (ANT +10.98%), the corporation behind Claude that recently went public, has contracted $161.2 billion in AI computing infrastructure from Broadcom, an agreement that runs for years and is largely non-cancellable.

But Anthropic has previously expanded a deal with Broadcom, and we may see more expansions in the future if demand for Anthropic's services accelerates. Further, Broadcom could continue to benefit from the ongoing race to develop increasingly sophisticated AI models. Meanwhile, the company expects $115 billion in AI semiconductor revenue for its fiscal year 2027 and $230 billion for its fiscal year 2028, and this isn't just wishful thinking.

The company has the deals in place to achieve this guidance. That's another reason why Broadcom's medium-term outlook is attractive. Investors should consider buying this stock and holding it through 2031.

AMD, a leader in CPU (central processing unit) technology, has also posted exceptional financial results. In the third quarter, the company's revenue increased by 45% year over year to $13.4 billion. Data center revenue grew 97% year over year to $8.5 billion. AMD's non-GAAP EPS was $2.09, up 74% compared to the year-ago period. Rising demand for CPUs, especially due to the agentic AI revolution, is driving much of that growth. And there is more where that came from.

AI agents are slowly gaining traction as they can help companies automate various tasks and become more efficient and more productive. That means lower costs, all else being equal, and higher profits. AMD is capitalizing on this boom, which may still just be getting started. The company estimates that its server CPU total addressable market will grow by about 50% annually through 2030, reaching $220 billion.

But management estimates that AMD's addressable opportunity across its entire business exceeds $1 trillion. There is plenty of competition, to be clear. But AMD has significant advantages, having been a leader in this market for decades. It owns one of the largest market shares and benefits from a wide moat thanks to switching costs. AMD's shares have slid in recent weeks, but given the company's opportunities, investors should consider buying the dip.

#2933. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in new wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year. Overall, Mehta expects Chevron to report Q3 2026 EPS of $4.95, above the consensus of $4.89.

"While unfavorable timing effects and volatile commodity prices may present quarterly earnings headwinds, we highlight healthy U.S. refining margins and strong asset utilization as partial offsets," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 381 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Chevron KPIs on TipRanks.

Kinetik Holdings (KNTK) is a fully integrated, pure-play, midstream company operating in the Delaware Basin. Earlier this month, the company declared a dividend of $0.81 per share, payable on October 30, 2026. With an annualized dividend of $3.24 per share, KNTK offers a yield of 5.82%. Kinetik will announce its Q3 earnings on November 4, with a conference call scheduled the next day.

Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst John Mackay reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and slightly raised his price target to $58 from $57. He expects the company to report Q3 2026 EBITDA of $279 million, higher than the Street's expectation of $270 million but lower than the second quarter's EBITDA of $281 million.

The 5-star analyst expects Kinetik's Q3 performance to gain from higher gas volumes after notable curtailments in the second quarter. Mackay also expects the quarter to benefit from higher production and steady commodity margins, even though some lower-margin contracts and weaker Waha spread marketing gains could weigh on results.

Overall, Mackay increased his Q3 2026 estimates to reflect higher volumes, driven by rapid Permian egress pipeline commissioning, stronger throughput at Kings Landing I, and higher M2M commodity prices, offset by increased costs.

"As natural gas takeaway constraints ease across the Permian, investor focus centers on KNTK's YE26 volume trajectory and durability of its multi-year growth," said Mackay.

Mackay ranks No. 569 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.9%. See Kinetik's Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving to Crescent Energy (CRGY), an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian, and Uinta Basins. With a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share (annualized dividend of $0.48 per share), CRGY's dividend yield stands at 3.56%. Earlier this month, Crescent announced an agreement to acquire Eagle Ford assets from Devon Energy (DVN).

Heading into Q3 earnings on Nov. 2, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reiterated a buy rating on Crescent stock and slightly lowered the price target to $17 from $18, citing dilution from new shares.

"CRGY's recent acquisition of DVN's Eagle Ford assets marks a strategic, growth-oriented move, potentially enhancing cash flow performance," said Richardson.

The 5-star analyst noted that the acquisition of the Eagle Ford assets at a net purchase price of $3.85 billion will add about 68 MBoe/d of net production and over 600 net Tier 1 locations. Richardson added that a solid track record of synergies from past deals in the Eagle Ford region increases confidence about Crescent achieving efficiencies with this deal.

Additionally, Richardson noted that the financial implications of the acquisition seem impressive, with a projected increase in cash flow per share of about 9% for 2027 to 2029.

The analyst believes that Crescent is not just expanding its business through acquisitions but positioning itself as a more durable company, regardless of market conditions.

Richardson ranks No. 478 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Crescent Energy Statistics on TipRanks.

I think a lot of people are wringing their hands about that. But today, we still have earnings to talk about. Tyler Crowe: Lou, I think the lesson here is always beat low expectations rather than miss high expectations, and I think that's one of the themes we could say here about Disney in this quarter.

Lou Whiteman: Absolutely. If you are bad enough for long enough, expectations become your friend. Is that the way you want to put it? Look, great news here. But what is the core business here to Matt's point? Because the entertainment business just still doesn't look that attractive to me. Focused to be single-digit operating income growth into the next year. As Matt said, they're no longer even reporting streaming separately, which I take to be they don't want to report streaming separately. I just don't think this model works, period. Lou Whiteman: Has anybody figured out entertainment or streaming or the post network world? We used to say Netflix had, but recent data would suggest maybe they haven't figured it out. Tyler Crowe: Content is always a challenge because people are always looking for new things, so it's not like you build a factory, and you can run that factory for 30 years and expect a cash stream. There's very rare that a company's core customer has around the clock access to the media and a tendency to point fingers, but that is what politicians do right or wrong. In all these cases, there's probably at least kernels of truth that the companies could have done better, and so I don't want to be too Pollyanna or too defensive. But right or wrong, just understand if you're going to invest in defense companies, you are asking for situations like this where somebody needs to paint a target and they are the obvious targets.

Maybe this brings to attention, a lot of investors being like, maybe I should have a little bit more exposure to defense, especially the better operators. Let's just put L3Harris aside. Guys, just a quick pitch on the way out. If you were to pitch an alternative stock in the National Security defense sphere of businesses, who are you pitching right now? Matt, you go first.

Matt Frankel: You're not going to want to hear this, and this is an outside the box pitch, but I'm going to double down on Kratos Defense. The drone company. First of all, I feel like it's ironic that L3Harris, their whole thesis is space and missiles, and they're being punished over a malfunctioning router. But Kratos, they've been beaten down. They spiked at the beginning of the Iran War. They're doing everything right. They're getting great government contracts. They're a big part of the Golden Dome. The valuation is really starting to make sense here, which that was everybody's biggest complaint back then, the business wasn't executing. It was valuation, and now I feel like that problem is largely gone away.

Tyler Crowe: All right. What's a ticker on Kratos?

Lou Whiteman: Matt, went higher risk, higher reward, so I will go the opposite just to more stayed. Northrop Grumman, ticker NOC is responsible for 2/3 of a nuclear triad. That's our greatest defense priority. That's what keeps people from bombing us because we can bomb them back. They're replacing the Minutemen; they're replacing the bombers. These are the biggest Pentagon priorities. They are pardon the pun bulletproof, whatever happens in Houston, Washington, and so I think slow and steady Northrop Grumman looks really good right now.

TL;DR: Rising inflation could, counterintuitively, help push mortgage rates further down.

Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 33 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates. But depending on how markets react, we could actually see lower mortgage rates. Keep reading after the charts for all the details.

Below are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for perspective.

P.S. Markets will be closed tomorrow for Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, and mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Like I mentioned above, it's not totally obvious where mortgage rates will head next. Let's walk through the two scenarios.

Here's why rates could go up: This morning, we got October's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, also known as PCE. It's the last measure of inflation to come out each month, but it's also the Federal Reserve's preferred metric, so PCE gets a lot of attention.

The stats came in mostly as predicted, though it's not like the predictions were good — inflation's been overly strong for a while. But the core year-over-year figure, which came in a tenth of a percent over predictions, could prove troublesome. Core PCE removes categories that can be extra volatile, so it's considered a measure that shows the underlying trend. In this case, the underlying trend is Not Good.

It's already pretty much a lock that we'll see a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, because yes, raising the federal funds rate is the Fed's main tool for taming inflation. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but a rate-hiking cycle from the central bankers definitely keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs.

On the other hand, here's why that same inflation data could help rates go down: Over the past several days, we've watched the stock market go on a wild ride, with the Anthropic IPO and the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Yesterday, things weren't looking good for tech stocks, and these inflation numbers could make it even worse.

The amount that tech companies have borrowed to fund AI buildout is a significant concern for investors, since companies will have to cover those costs before investors see any profits. It's already a big task, and if everything costs more thanks to inflation, it's that much harder.

This AI-related anxiety is rough on the stock market, but it's been a boon for Treasury bonds. More demand for bonds pushes up bond prices, which brings down bond yields (basically, the return investors get on a bond). Mortgage rates for 30-year loans are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, so here's why you care about all of this: Lower Treasury yields means lower mortgage rates, too. If investors keep stressing about inflation eating into tech profits, we could see mortgage rates continue to move lower.

That was a lot of info on inflation, but inflation's not the only major metric influencing rates.

Let's back up for a second. The Federal Reserve tries to keep the economy steady by focusing on two key goals, often referred to as the Fed's dual mandate. One side is price stability — keeping inflation reasonable. The other is maximum employment, meaning those who want to work are able to find jobs.

Next week we'll shift our focus to the employment side of the Federal Reserve's mandate, because the first week of the month is always all about employment data. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, we'll kick things off with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). JOLTS can tip us off to trends in the labor market; stuff like whether folks are leaving jobs voluntarily or if companies have openings that are going unfilled.

On Wednesday, payroll firm ADP will release its monthly employment stats. ADP is looking at its own payroll data to get an idea of how the job market is growing or contracting. The numbers don't include the public sector, but ADP often provides a preview of how the jobs report will go.

The Employment Situation Summary, better known as the jobs report, drops on Friday. This is the big one, since it tells us the nation's unemployment rate. The jobs report's other major stat is, similar to ADP, how many jobs the economy added or lost in the previous month. Unlike ADP though, the jobs report is inclusive of everybody in the public and private sectors.

Lately the labor market's been looking super healthy, which is great news for the economy but less positive for mortgage rates. When hiring's strong, the Fed can feel safer raising the federal funds rate (that's the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers adjust). Higher rates tend to discourage businesses from borrowing and expanding, so if the job market's on shaky footing, the central bankers are going to be cautious about raising the benchmark rate.

What we're seeing now though, where inflation is clearly the problem and employment's just fine, is a recipe for higher rates. Again, the Fed doesn't control mortgage rates, but the central bank being in rate-hike mode puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

If we were to see employment falter in this latest round of numbers, it still probably wouldn't change the Fed's plan. That would be one poor month for the labor market versus months upon months of inflation running rampant — so yeah, they'll keep an eye on jobs, but inflation's still the scourge.

Our most likely source of lower mortgage rates in the short term is what I described above; investors who are leery of inflation and the promise of AI looking to the safe harbor of the bond market.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.55% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

» Stay informed: Check out NerdWallet's mortgage news hub for all our latest coverage.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#2928. Advance Auto Parts vs. Shopify: Which Retail Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Shopify's 32.5% revenue jump and debt-free balance sheet stand in sharp contrast to Advance Auto Parts' flat sales and heavy leverage, but valuation may tip the scales.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 28, 2026 at 1:10PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Advance Auto Parts ›

Investors today face a choice between a legacy retailer undergoing a strategic shift and a high-growth technology platform. Choosing between Advance Auto Parts (AAP -0.76%) and Shopify (SHOP +6.28%) requires weighing turnaround potential against scaling infrastructure.

Advance Auto Parts focuses on the physical automotive aftermarket, while Shopify provides the digital plumbing for modern global commerce. This comparison examines their financial health, growth trajectories, and valuation multiples to help you decide which fits your 2027 goals.

Advance Auto Parts is a major provider of automotive aftermarket parts, serving two distinct customer segments. About 50% of its sales come from professional installers, such as garages and dealerships, while the remainder serves do-it-yourself enthusiasts. The company also supports more than 800 independently owned Carquest-branded stores, providing a broad footprint across North America and the Caribbean.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 10, 2026, the company generated revenue of approximately $8.6 billion, representing a slight decline of about 0.3% compared to the prior period. Despite this flat growth, it reported GAAP net income of about $100 million. This performance comes as the company navigates a competitive retail environment and focuses on internal efficiencies to stabilize its bottom line.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, Advance Auto Parts carries a debt-to-equity ratio of about 2.4x. This metric indicates that the company uses about $2.40 in total debt per dollar of shareholder equity. Its current ratio of 1.7x indicates a healthy ability to cover short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 3, 2026, free cash flow was negative $298 million, highlighting the capital-intensive nature of its current operations.

Shopify has established itself as a dominant force among tech stocks by offering an all-in-one commerce platform. It serves millions of merchants in over 175 countries, ranging from individual entrepreneurs to massive enterprise brands. The business model is highly diversified, with no single merchant accounting for more than 5% of total revenues, which reduces reliance on any single client.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, Shopify achieved revenue of approximately $14.2 billion, which is a significant increase of about 32.5% over the previous year. The company reported GAAP net income of about $2.1 billion during this time frame. This robust growth suggests that Shopify continues to capture a larger share of the global commerce market as more businesses move their operations online.

Shopify maintains an exceptionally strong balance sheet as of December 2025, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x. This indicates the company has no debt relative to its equity, while its current ratio of 6.0x shows an abundance of liquid assets to cover liabilities. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, it generated $2.0 billion in free cash flow. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 22% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Advance Auto Parts operates in a highly competitive environment featuring national chains like AutoZone (AZO -0.15%) and O'Reilly Automotive (ORLY -0.42%). The company faces risks from global supply chain disruptions and potential tariffs that could increase costs. Additionally, its significant total debt may limit financial flexibility if macroeconomic conditions like inflation or high fuel costs further dampen consumer discretionary spending on vehicle repairs.

Shopify contends with fierce competition in commerce services and relies on third-party partners like Alphabet (GOOGL +0.68%) for cloud hosting. It also depends on relationships with Stripe and PayPal (PYPL +2.30%) for payment processing, which adds a layer of external dependency. Furthermore, the company must manage risks related to security breaches of merchant data and the volatility of its share price in an evolving regulatory landscape for digital commerce.

Shopify carries a much higher price relative to its sales and future earnings estimates compared to the lower multiples found at Advance Auto Parts.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

The Forward P/E ratio compares the stock price to future earnings estimates over the next year. The P/S ratio measures the market capitalization against sales over the past twelve months.

Advance Auto Parts is in the midst of turning around the struggles it has experienced over the past few years, including sales growth, margins, and market share. The aftermarket auto parts business has been in a slump, largely due to a mix of factors: weak do-it-yourself demand, vehicle electrification, intense competition, and general pocketbook pressures on consumers.

Company management has been addressing the business's issues by rolling out a new multi-year turnaround program. That started in late 2024, including closing stores, optimizing store footprints, and overhauling its supply chain--for instance, reducing the number of carriers by 70% through consolidated shipments. To date, the turnaround program has had mixed success. The first quarter of fiscal 2026 delivered results well above expectations: revenue of $2.6 billion and net income of $25 million. The second quarter and third quarter disappointed. In the third quarter, reported in early November, the company disappointed on revenue, with just over $2 billion in sales and net income of $15 million. Revenue was slightly below the year-ago quarter, while the business swung from a net loss in the same period.

Analysts see full-year 2026 sales slightly lower year-over-year at around $8.5 billion, with net income improving to around $132 million, more than three times 2025.

Shopify is also coming off an excellent quarterly report, tallying third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $3.74 billion, up 32% year over year. It's the business's fourth quarter in a row with more than $3 billion in revenue, a mark it first reached in 2025. It is interesting to note that the business is growing much faster than the retail industry it serves.

Shopify appears ready to benefit from the age of agentic AI merchandising, which is just getting off the ground. Shopify supports the UCP from Google, designed to enable agentic AI commerce by allowing AI agents to interact with merchant systems throughout the shopping journey. That, along with other trends, has management projecting low-30% annual revenue growth for the current year. Long-term, management aims to expand in Europe to drive additional growth.

Shopify comes at a premium, but its tech stack and potential for further growth give it the nod over Advance Auto Parts, which, while having some success in its turnaround, isn't a lock to deliver a transformative 2027.

#2926. Ready for ‘The Great Lock In’? Viral Money Trend Can Improve Focus

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Winter is the ideal time to make progress on your financial goals.

When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.

That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

“You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”

One important component of the Great Lock In is developing new routines that will last well into 2027, says Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

“We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he says. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”

Ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

What’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

“Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird says. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”

Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman says.

If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the new saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

“It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

Once you’ve outlined those big goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird says.

He suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

Baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he says.

Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird says.

“Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he says. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

Baird says that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

Mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he says. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”

Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

With credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird says. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.)

“High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman says. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

Even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

“It’s like a diet,” Baird says. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”

“Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he says.

In fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he says. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”

#2924. Jensen Huang's Return as CEO Doesn't Fix All of Nvidia's Problems, but It Gives It a Fighting Chance

Huang's reinstatement is great news for the chipmaker, but issues remain.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 28, 2026 at 1:11PM EST

Jensen Huang's return to the helm of Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%) less than two weeks after he resigned was sweet music to the ears of investors, who sent the stock and the entire market skyrocketing on the news. While his reinstatement as CEO does not solve all the company's problems, its importance should not be underestimated.

Let's look at some of the issues Nvidia still faces and Huang's importance.

While Huang has apparently had several extramarital affairs, it was his involvement with Alice Huang (no relation), a tech exec who previously led a Singapore-based cloud company — and an alleged Chinese spy — that ultimately led to his resignation. However, President Donald Trump lobbied hard for Nvidia to bring him back, saying he posed no threat to national security and that the U.S. had to protect its geniuses. That said, the company continues to face multiple investigations relating both to chip smuggling and accounting fraud.

Alice Huang, her associate Li Ming, Singapore cloud computing company Megaspeed, and Super Micro Computer (SMCI +1.93%) are all reportedly being investigated for smuggling Nvidia GPUs to China. Meanwhile, Nvidia itself has not been cleared, with the U.S. government still investigating which employees at Nvidia knew that its products were likely being sold to Chinese entities.

Even if Nvidia didn't violate any laws, there is a risk that its indirect business in China would be affected by a further crackdown from Washington. This includes not just chips exported to China but also to data center operators outside China that provide services to Chinese AI companies to train their models.

A bit lost amid the Nvidia scandal is perhaps a risk even greater to the company. In the middle of the controversy, Anthropic (ANT +10.98%) revealed that its Claude Mythos models could help other models running on Nvidia GPUs switch to Advanced Micro Devices' (AMD +4.56%) GPUs in just a few days, with barely any human input needed. Up until now, adjusting the software for that type of switch has been a monumental task that would take up to a year and a dozen engineers. Anthropic said this breakthrough was part of its fungible chip strategy that lets it focus on chip price performance and use chips based on availability and what they do best.

This comes at a bad time for Nvidia. First, many of its hyperscaler customers have designed their own custom chips, which can handle their specific AI workloads at lower costs. Semianalysis has reported that Alphabet's (GOOGL +0.68%) (GOOG +0.54%) custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) are now outperforming Nvidia's GPUs on a price-performance basis. At the same time, AMD just released its Helios service rack, which is based around its latest GPUs and CPUs, competes on power with Nvidia's new Vera Rubin architecture, and is much cheaper. AMD has multiple big orders from hyperscalers, and if Helios performs well, it could gain market share.

In a world where AI data center chips are truly fungible, there is a serious risk that Nvidia's pricing power could erode, which could significantly compress gross margins and hurt profitability.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

While the risks for Nvidia are rising, having Huang back at the helm is a huge boost. He is one of the best CEOs on the planet and has a gift for seeing where the tech sector is headed before most.

Huang has been very aware of the risk of chip fungibility, which is one reason the company is now selling rack solutions rather than just GPUs, and a major reason it created its own open-source Nemotron AI models and acquired companies like Hugging Face and SchedMD.

Nvidia is quietly looking to lead the charge on open-source AI models, which, through its recent acquisitions, are becoming optimized for its systems. This comes at a time when the enterprise segment has increasingly turned to cheaper open-source AI models rather than more expensive ones from Anthropic and OpenAI.

This is basically a battle of whether chips or AI models become commoditized. Luckily for Nvidia shareholders, the company just brought back the man with the vision to help it win this battle.

#2922. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2921. Himax: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Wafer-level optics give Himax a precision edge in co-packaged optics, a bet that could matter more than the near-term automotive dip.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 28, 2026 at 1:19PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Himax Technologies ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Himax (HIMX +7.84%) announced third quarter revenue of $246.8 million. A short-term inventory pullback in automotive displays masks expanding design wins in optical technologies and edge artificial intelligence. Three things management said stand out.

Chinese car exporters overbuilt display inventory following rapid overseas expansion, forcing panel makers to trim fourth-quarter orders. The underlying demand holds as vehicle display content expands across larger screens and head-up displays.

Wafer-level optics (WLO, a semiconductor manufacturing process for etching microlenses on glass wafers) give the business a precision edge in optical components for co-packaged optics (CPO, an architecture that integrates optical interfaces directly with silicon chips). Precision manufacturing creates entry barriers that traditional optical assembly can't match.

WiseEye artificial intelligence microprocessors (ultra-low-power chips designed for continuous visual sensing on battery-powered devices) consume just a few milliwatts during operation. High-profile customer deployments validate the technology's energy efficiency and expand sales into non-driver product categories.

Foundry price hikes for legacy chip nodes tighten supply chain costs into 2027. Prioritizing securing foundry capacity and rising sales of display timing controllers (Tcons, chips that manage screen timing and pixel data) position the business to defend profitability.

Increasing display content per vehicle and optical commercialization support revenue growth in 2027, with non-driver products approaching 30% of total sales.

#2917. Anthropic Is Headed for the Nasdaq-100. Here's What That Means for QQQ Investors.

This ETF's shareholders are about to own the Claude maker, whether they buy it on purpose or not.

By Neil Patel – Nov 28, 2026 at 1:21PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

The market has cooled on Anthropic (ANT +10.98%). The Claude maker's shares tumbled 6.5% on Nov. 24, and they’re 26.5% below the opening price from the initial public offering (IPO) on Nov. 19.

Nonetheless, the dominant artificial intelligence (AI) model developer sports a massive market capitalization of just under $1.1 trillion. It took less than six years after founding to become one of the world's most valuable companies, establishing how powerful the AI boom has been. This size puts Anthropic in the fast lane to be included in a major index sooner rather than later.

This AI stock is headed for the Nasdaq-100. Here's what that means for investors in the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ +2.69%).

New listings usually need to wait. Nasdaq (NDAQ +1.93%) historically required at least three full calendar months of trading before a company could join the Nasdaq-100. That changed on May 1 this year.

Under the new fast-entry rule, a newly listed company qualifies if its full market cap ranks within the top 40 of current index members. It must also pass other tests, like being a non-financial business. Nasdaq checks the ranking after the seventh trading day. The addition to the index typically happens after the 15th trading day.

Anthropic passes the test with ease. The top-40 cutoff was roughly $100 billion at the end of 2025, according to Nasdaq. The AI lab is worth about 10 times that.

Anthropic's seventh trading day will be Nov. 30. That day lines up with the reference date for Nasdaq's annual December reshuffle. Bloomberg reports that Anthropic is on track to join at the open on Dec. 21.

Nothing is official yet. But Nasdaq President Nelson Griggs said on Nov. 19 that the company will be evaluated for the top 40, "which clearly it looks like they will be." He added that the final call depends on where the market cap goes. Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.83%) took this same path in July. Assuming the latest IPO stock doesn't collapse, Anthropic should qualify.

For Invesco QQQ Trust investors, Anthropic will simply show up in their portfolios. The exchange-traded fund (ETF), with $451 billion in assets, must buy shares at the market price. A fast-entry addition doesn't force Nasdaq to kick any business out. The fund makes room by trimming every other holding slightly.

Don't expect a giant position, though. Only a small slice of Anthropic trades publicly. The IPO sold 980 million shares out of roughly 13.2 billion outstanding. For low-float stocks like this, Nasdaq caps the weight at 3 times the freely tradable shares. Estimates for the company's starting weight sit under 1%. The fund's top 10 holdings, by comparison, make up 46% of assets.

This overall impact sounds minor. QQQ investors already own more Anthropic than they might initially assume, however. Amazon (AMZN +3.96%) owns 14.7% of Anthropic, and Alphabet (GOOGL +0.68%) (GOOG +0.54%) holds 13.7%. Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.60%) were among the group that bought $26 billion of shares in a private placement. These "Magnificent Seven" stocks are also holdings in the ETF.

Investors will gain exposure to a high-powered name. Anthropic's revenue hit $33.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 13-fold. You'd struggle to find any business on Earth that has grown this fast at this scale.

There are risks to consider. No one knows how much economic value the AI models will capture in the long run. Anthropic isn't yet profitable on a generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) basis, and it has enormous spending commitments. Customer concentration and an entangled AI ecosystem create deep dependencies.

Still, one holding at an expected 1% weight won't make or break a 100-plus stock ETF. The biggest positions will keep driving returns. A sound long-term strategy doesn't need to change because of one new name.

Invesco QQQ Trust shareholders should stay the course.

#2916. 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

You don’t need a basement bunker, but keeping some cash on hand might help.

If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

But what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

Dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he said in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”

Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:

Last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, says Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

If systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, said Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good plan, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?)

“My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson said. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”

If your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

“This is the step I push hardest,” Judge says. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”

If you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” says Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”

Make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

Keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

Take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

And set a reminder to update your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the big concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he says. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

“The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” said Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”
