#2914. Prediction: This Will Be Anthropic Stock's Price in 1 Year

By Jennifer Saibil – Nov 28, 2026 at 1:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

After soaring to $111 on its first day of trading, it sank back 10% on the second day. There's likely some volatility ahead, and the price could be different by the time this is published. Let's see where Anthropic stock could be in one year.

Anthropic is the company behind Claude, the leading AI model, and it's growing like wildfire. Revenue increased more than 1,200% year over year in the third quarter as it monetized the chatbot, and it has close to 12,000 customers paying at least $100,000, up from 400 in March 2025. As of now, five single clients account for about 20% of total revenue, which means the loss of one could significantly affect it. However, that has shrunk from about 35% in the first quarter, and as it grows, it becomes less dependent on any specific client.

Management sees all sorts of use cases for its technology beyond the corporate. It's structured as a public benefit corporation, which means that it sees its business as having public benefit beyond making profits. It envisions being able to cure "diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases." CEO Dario Amodei even said, "I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years," in a post on X.

Revenue increased from $41 million in 2023 to more than $4 billion in 2025, or 10x in only three years, and it already has $33 billion for the first nine months of 2026. Wall Street expects revenue to increase 132% in 2027, a steep slowdown, but still rapid growth.

Anthropic is spending a lot of money on growth, with the belief that it needs to scale to demonstrate its most potent results. It has major commitments for compute power with Space Exploration Technologies, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and the gamut of top AI companies. Its total is more than $800 billion, but that goes as far as 2036.

Capital expenditures for the first nine months of 2026 were $925 million, and Anthropic reported a $1.3 billion operating loss. However, it notes that it's operating efficiently, and while revenue grew double digits in Q3, headcount only increased 170%. Things are already improving, and the adjusted operating margin was 15% in Q3, up from a 93% adjusted operating margin loss last year.

As Anthropic scales efficiently, it will get closer to profitability, but much of this thesis depends on continued growth in AI. There's a chance that development will slow down as regulations increase, and Anthropic faces tough competition from OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, and more.

However, Wall Street expects $0.55 in earnings per share next year, implying that Anthropic will report a net profit.

For all the hype, Wall Street doesn't see incredible gains happening this year. The average consensus target price is a 50% gain over the next 12 to 18 months. Don't get me wrong, that's a great return, but it's not earth-shattering. Even the highest price target is 74% higher than today's price.

Anthropic stock currently trades at 33 times trailing 12-month sales. If it keeps that ratio and doubles sales, the stock would double, too. The lower price targets are likely because if revenue slows from four digits to three digits, it will have a lower price-to-sales ratio. If the ratio goes down to about two-thirds of where it is today, or a multiple of 22, and revenue doubles to $70 billion, the market cap would be $1.5 trillion, or about 29% higher than today's.

The company facilitates more than 9 million active listings across 220 countries and regions. By focusing on a marketplace model rather than owning properties, the company maintains an asset-light strategy that supports high profitability and broad geographic reach.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $13.9 billion, which represents growth of approximately 16.7%. During this same period, the company generated GAAP net income of about $3.2 billion. This financial performance highlights the company's ability to scale its global platform while maintaining a net margin of approximately 23%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is about 0.3x. This ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, suggests a conservative use of borrowed capital. The current ratio, a measure of whether a company can cover its short-term debts with short-term assets, stands at about 1.4x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was about $4.6 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) accounted for roughly 34.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Chewy serves approximately 21.3 million active customers by providing a wide range of pet products, prescriptions, and veterinary services. Its business model thrives on its Autoship subscription program, which helps ensure steady, predictable revenue from pet owners who need regular supplies. The company also manages physical 'Chewy Vet Care' clinics and the PracticeHub platform, which integrates with approximately 20,000 veterinary practices.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 2, 2026, revenue reached about $13.1 billion, representing growth of approximately 5.9%. During this period, the company reported GAAP net income of about $273.7 million. While the company operates with a relatively modest net margin of about 2.1%, it has successfully transitioned from a high-growth start-up to a profitable e-commerce leader.

As of its February 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is about 1.0x. This indicates that total debt is approximately equal to shareholder equity. The current ratio is about 0.9x, indicating that its short-term liabilities are slightly higher than its short-term assets. In the fiscal year ended Feb. 1, 2026, free cash flow was about $562.4 million. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 43.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Airbnb faces an evolving landscape of complex and fragmented short-term rental laws, including outright bans in major cities like New York. The company is also managing significant ongoing tax disputes in Italy and the U.S. regarding the valuation of its intellectual property. Furthermore, it faces intense pressure from major hotel chains and online travel agencies such as Booking Holdings (BKNG +0.59%) and Expedia Group (EXPE +2.22%).

Chewy is dependent on an efficient supply chain and its own network of fulfillment centers, where any disruption could severely impact operations. The company competes in a highly crowded pet retail industry against massive e-commerce players like Amazon (AMZN +3.96%) and various brick-and-mortar retailers. Additionally, Chewy relies on third-party shipping and cloud providers, making it vulnerable to service interruptions that could lead to fulfillment delays.

Chewy appears more attractively valued based on its Forward P/E and P/S ratio, though Airbnb generates significantly higher profits and cash flow.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Airbnb reported an excellent third quarter of fiscal 2026, typically its strongest period of the year, beating consensus revenue estimates by some $120 million, reporting $4.87 billion in sales, up 19% from the same period in 2025, driven by a strong increase in booked nights. North America bookings grew at their fastest rate in four years, while growth accelerated in its other major markets, the U.K., France, and Australia.

The business is finding ways to expand its popular travel business, embracing features like buy now, pay later (BNPL) on reservations, a form of short-term lending. Management has also seen great success getting hotels onto its platform, and says 35% of new Airbnb customers are booking hotels through it. The network advantage of Airbnb's history, over 2 billion guest arrivals since 2008, and the lack of host presence on AI (meaning a competitor using AI has little data to scrape to form a competing product) give it a competitive moat.

For the full year, Wall Street expects sales of $14.4 billion with net income of $3.3 billion.

Chewy is establishing a steady growth pattern. In a recently reported quarter, management noted that its Autoship program grew faster than overall sales, implying that many customers' standing orders will continue to provide a solid base for the company. The company also believes that in the long run, veterinarian and general pet health services are a huge untapped market for Chewy. The business recently closed on the acquisition of Modern Animal, which delivers high profitability per location and is a strong complement to Chewy's existing business.

For fiscal 2027, sales are seen rising 7% to $13.5 billion, with net income up more than 40% to around $317 million, according to consensus analyst estimates. American consumers have shown they will spend up to take care of their pets.

However, Chewy likely doesn't have a great competitive moat against brick-and-mortar competitors like PetSmart and Petco Health and Wellness Co Inc. (WOOF +0.00%).

Going into 2027, there's little to dislike about Airbnb, but for one thing: its valuation. At nearly 32x forward earnings, shares are pricey and considerably higher than competitors like Booking Holdings. Chewy offers a more defensive profile given the success of its Autoship program. At a more reasonable P/E, go with Chewy.

#2900. 3 Signs a Roth IRA Is the Best Place for Your Retirement Savings in 2027

The decision to use a Roth IRA or not could have a significant effect on your retirement finances.

By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 28, 2026 at 2:00PM EST

With just a few weeks left until 2027, now is a great time to start planning where you want to put your retirement savings next year. The account(s) you use will affect how much you're allowed to save, what you can invest in, and your future tax bills.

A Roth IRA is one popular option worth considering. It's not the right choice for everyone, but if these three things apply to you, it could be a good fit.

Roth IRAs have income limits that prevent high earners from contributing directly. These limits vary by year and your tax filing status.

If you're a single adult or a head of household who expects to earn less than $158,000 next year, or a married couple that expects to earn less than $250,000, you're in the clear. You can contribute up to the $7,500 annual contribution limit if you're under 50, or the $8,600 limit if you'll be 50 or older by Dec. 31, 2027.

Single adults and heads of household earning between $158,000 and $173,000 and married couples earning between $250,000 and $260,000 in 2027 will be eligible to contribute a reduced amount. If you earn more than $173,000 as a single adult or head of household or $260,000 as a married couple, you may not contribute to a Roth IRA directly next year.

Roth IRAs require you to pay taxes on your contributions upfront, but then you're allowed to take tax-free withdrawals from these accounts in retirement.

This strategy makes the most sense if you expect to be in the same or a higher tax bracket in retirement than the one you're in right now. If you anticipate your income dropping significantly in retirement, you might prefer to use a traditional IRA instead.

This gives you an upfront tax break when you make your contributions, but you owe taxes on your withdrawals later. If you're in a lower tax bracket in retirement, you might lose a smaller percentage of your savings than you would have by paying taxes now.

Roth accounts are the only ones that offer tax-free withdrawals in retirement. This gives you greater control over your retirement tax bills. If you find yourself nearing the top of your tax bracket one year, you can rely more on your Roth withdrawals for the remainder of the year to get the money you need without jumping up to the next tax bracket.

If this appeals to you, it could be worth stashing some money in a Roth IRA in 2027. If you max that out and want to set aside even more in Roth accounts, check whether your employer offers a Roth 401(k). These work similar to traditional 401(k)s, except you fund them with after-tax dollars.

While both serve the modern enterprise, they occupy very different niches within the software ecosystem.

Fastly operates an edge cloud platform designed to help developers build, secure, and deliver digital experiences closer to their end users. The company serves global organizations through its content delivery network and security services, counting high-profile names like TikTok among its enterprise customers. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is 2.6x, measuring the company's ability to cover short-term obligations with its short-term assets. The debt-to-equity ratio is about 0.5x, comparing total debt to the value of shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was around $65.8 million. Monday.com provides a flexible AI workspace platform that enables teams to manage projects, marketing campaigns, and customer relationships in a single interface. The company has rapidly expanded its footprint among tech stocks by catering to approximately 250,000 customers worldwide across hundreds of industries. Its strategy focuses on moving upmarket to larger enterprise clients while maintaining a user-friendly experience that requires minimal technical expertise.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $1.4 billion, which represents revenue growth of approximately 22.4% over the previous year. This growth is supported by a net income of around $143.4 million, showing the company's ability to generate positive returns as it scales. The net margin is about 10%, indicating that the company is effectively retaining a portion of its sales as profit after accounting for all expenses.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is 2.5x. The debt-to-equity ratio is about 0.3x, suggesting a conservative level of debt relative to equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached approximately $309.9 million. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) accounted for roughly 53.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Fastly faces intense competition from established providers like Akamai Technologies (AKAM +2.21%) and large cloud incumbents including Amazon (AMZN +3.96%), Microsoft (MSFT +0.60%), and Alphabet (GOOG +0.54%). The company faces significant revenue concentration, leaving it vulnerable if major clients reduce usage or switch providers. Monday.com operates in a highly competitive market for workflow and project management tools, where it must continually innovate to differentiate itself from rivals such as Microsoft. The company faces the challenge of maintaining its high growth rates as it expands into more of the enterprise market and navigates shifting corporate spending priorities. Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Monday.com is undergoing a bit of a reset. In July, it fired 20% of its workforce. It's part of an effort to redirect more capital to AI services for its platform.

In its third quarter, revenue grew 19% year-over-year to nearly $378 million, with net income of $35.2 million.

There were bright spots when looking under the hood of top-line results. Management touted a record net addition of $100,000-plus and $500,000-plus (client spending) customers, saying they reflect the continued strength of Monday.com's push to go upmarket. Fastly processes over 5 trillion requests a day, a huge number that is actually just a small part of the total addressable market (TAM) for the business. Management sees the TAM as $22 billion, giving it a long runway for growth. The company has posted three straight quarters of more than 20% growth (year-over-year).

One of the company's competitive edges, it says, is that it dynamically allocates its resources in real time to match the global load. So, for example, one Thursday night, its network might be delivering Thursday Night Football. On Black Friday, the exact same network is handling e-commerce. The next week, it might be handling a video game release. Fastly says that makes it a much more efficient network than competitors' siloed networks for security, compute, and delivery, et cetera.

For the current fiscal year, look for sales to grow to $747 million, a 20% rise over the prior year, with a much narrower net loss of about $56 million.

Ordinarily, Monday.com's fast growth and low forward P/E would give it the nod, but the heavy firings of its workforce in July raise a red flag: is the business foreseeing long-term weakness, or did management so poorly manage its workforce beforehand that it was a bloated enterprise? Neither is good, if the case. AI efficiencies could very well account for the need to cut a fifth of the workforce, but it's better to wait and see that the business is executing before jumping in. For 2027, Fastly is the better buy.

#2888. Trump Just Proposed Another Round of Tariffs. Why the Timing Couldn't Be Worse for Wall Street.

The latest round of tariffs could spell bad news for some stocks with surprisingly little exposure to them.

By Steven Porrello – Nov 28, 2026 at 2:12PM EST

The stock market hardly needed another reason to worry. Yet here we go again. On Wednesday, Nov. 25, President Donald Trump's administration proposed a new round of tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan, India, South Korea, and the European Union.

The timing of these tariffs, which include an additional 20% on certain Chinese imports, could hardly be worse. That's an understatement: It's bad timing, very bad. Inflation is picking up again, another interest rate hike is becoming more likely, Wall Street has begun reconsidering artificial intelligence (AI), and the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.60%), Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +2.31%), and Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +1.18%), have all entered correction territory.

Geez, that's quite a lot for the market to digest. So why not add another round of tariffs?

As we learned in April 2025, when the S&P 500 shed roughly $5 trillion in market value in just two trading sessions following Trump's tariff announcement, Wall Street doesn’t take kindly to the prospect of tariffs. And yet what I find particularly concerning is that this round of tariffs could hurt stocks you might not think would be affected by them. Here's why.

First, it's worth remembering where we were a little over two years ago. In September 2024, the Federal Reserve began lowering interest rates after spending much of the previous two and a half years fighting inflation. It seemed like the battle was over, and though inflation wasn't yet at the Fed's 2% target, there was reason to believe it was moving in that direction.

On Wednesday, the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that inflation, as measured by the PCE price index, rose 3.8% year over year in October, up from 3.6% in September. That means inflation is not only running at nearly twice the Fed's target, but it's also moving further away from that target.

In this context, another round of tariffs could make inflation more stubborn. Tariffs often make it more expensive for businesses to import goods, as well as the materials and components they need to manufacture products. Although the inflationary effects of tariffs are somewhat complicated -- businesses, for example, might absorb some of the additional costs rather than raise prices -- to the extent that businesses pass those additional costs on to consumers, tariffs could put upward pressure on inflation.

What concerns me as a growth stock investor is that the longer inflation remains elevated, the longer inflation rates could remain elevated, too. In other words, even if this latest round of tariffs doesn't ultimately result in the Fed raising interest rates, it could delay the point at which the Fed feels comfortable lowering them again.

The thing about tariffs is that a company doesn't necessarily need to import anything for its stock to suffer from them. If the indirect effect of tariffs is that interest rates stay higher for longer, then some of the most vulnerable stocks could simply be those trading at high valuations.

To understand why, consider what happens when interest rates go up. Investors may be able to earn higher returns on relatively safe investments, like U.S. Treasury securities, and consequently may be less willing to pay a premium for the earnings a company might generate several years from now. That's particularly problematic for growth stocks, much of whose value is derived from earnings that haven't materialized yet.

In light of this, investors who are buying the dip in AI stocks should be particularly discerning right now. Rather than comparing a stock's current price to what it traded at six months ago, I'd compare its valuation with what I'd reasonably expect its business to earn over the next several years. At this point, I would also favor companies that generate enough cash to finance their own growth, as opposed to those that depend heavily on borrowing.

Undoubtedly, great investment opportunities exist in this market. But I'd be careful about buying stocks that require not only exceptional earnings growth but also an improvement in economic conditions to deliver decent returns.

#2887. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2882. VOO and VGT Cost Almost the Same. They Behave Very Differently.

Vanguard's tech ETF has turned $10,000 into about $75,300 in 10 years. What did its investors put up with to get there?

By Anders Bylund – Nov 28, 2026 at 2:21PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ›

Two Vanguard funds, both alike in dignity, charge 0.03% and 0.09% in annual fees. Yet, they feel like completely different investments.

The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +1.66%) and the Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT +2.51%) cost $3 and $9 a year per $10,000. Same sponsor, same bargain pricing, but wildly different personalities.

VOO, which tracks the S&P 500, holds 515 positions, and technology makes up roughly 37% of the portfolio. VGT holds 319 stocks, and the entire portfolio sits in the technology sector.

Apple (AAPL +0.83%), Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), and Microsoft (MSFT +0.60%) are the three largest holdings in both funds. Together they account for 21.2% of VOO and 46.8% of VGT. Semiconductors alone are 35.6% of VGT.

There's nothing wrong with VGT's extreme concentration, of course. It was built to do exactly this, and you can see it in the fund name.

Over the past 10 years, VGT delivered an annualized total return of 22.4%, compared with 14.5% for VOO. With dividends reinvested, $10,000 in each would have grown to about $75,300 in VGT and about $38,700 in VOO.

VGT's ride has been rougher. It has a beta of 1.4, meaning it has historically moved about 40% more than the market on average. As of Nov. 27, it sits 19.5% below its 52-week high, while VOO is 6.7% below its own.

VOO is the sturdy portfolio base: one broad fund for large U.S. companies. VGT is more like the seasoning on top, a smaller slice for investors who want more tech and can handle a 19.5% slide without selling. Owning both is fine, but that's not diversification. VOO already holds the same giants, just with different weightings. VGT mostly turns up the dial on tech-based potential and risk.

Both funds add a significant tech splash, and VGT is all about that flavor.

#2879. If a Bear Market Is Coming, This Is Warren Buffett's Time-Tested Strategy

Warren Buffett did three things, but the final step is often the hardest in a bear market.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 28, 2026 at 2:36PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›

Warren Buffett, the former CEO of Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.30%)(BRKB +0.25%), broke his investment approach down into three steps: find good companies, buy when the stock is attractively priced, and then hold for the long term. That sounds easy, but it isn't. And the hardest step of all is the one that requires you to do absolutely nothing. Here's why holding through a bear market is still likely to be the winning move.

Warren Buffett never described his investment approach in fine detail, preferring to give broad generalizations. That's actually good news for investors because it means his general approach can be applied across many styles, including growth, value, and income investing. But each step is still very important.

The first thing is to find good companies. That sets the foundation, but you may not be able to buy the companies you like right away because good companies often carry premium price tags. Which is why waiting for an attractive price is step two. It can require patience, but tracking valuation metrics can help you keep your enthusiasm in check until mercurial Wall Street provides a buying opportunity.

Then the really hard work starts because you have to hold for the long term. This is where Buffett's approach really shines, because his goal was to benefit from the long-term growth of the businesses he bought. It is hard to overstate how difficult it is to just do nothing as an investor. Wall Street is driven by activity, and simply sitting around can feel like you are missing out. If steps one and two are covered, you aren't missing anything by sitting back and watching the grass grow.

If Berkshire Hathaway's success isn't enough to prove the value of holding through thick and thin, then look at the S&P 500 index (^GSPC +1.60%) chart above. Notice the fairly frequent dips along the index's long upward path. Those are bear markets, with some of the most recent occurring during the dot-com crash, the Great Recession, and the coronavirus pandemic. The S&P 500 recovered after each downturn and reached new record highs.

In fact, Buffett even suggested that people looking to make investing as simple as possible skip steps one and two and just buy an S&P 500 index fund, such as Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +1.66%). The index is designed to represent the U.S. economy and is often referred to as "the market." So you guarantee yourself market returns by buying the S&P 500. That's more than enough to build material wealth over the long term if, here's the key, you hold for the long term.

Do not underestimate the difficulty of doing nothing. It is, perhaps, the hardest thing you have to do when you invest like Buffett. In bull markets, as noted, you'll feel like you should be doing more. The "fear of missing out" (FOMO) will make you want to buy and sell. In bear markets, it gets even worse. You will watch as your wealth slips away day after day, which may even elicit physical symptoms such as sleeplessness, mental distraction, and agita. If history is any guide, selling out of fear in a bear market is a mistake.

Buffett's basic approach of buying good companies when they are reasonably priced and holding for the long term is pretty universal. You can apply these basic premises to your own personal investment preferences. But the third step, holding, is likely to be the most important. It is hard to do nothing in bull markets, but even harder in bear markets. Which is why you should mentally prepare yourself now for the next downturn. Nobody knows when, but another bear market will show up sooner or later.

#2876. Docusign vs. UiPath: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Docusign's push beyond e-signatures meets UiPath's AI agents, and the valuation gap may matter more than either company's growth story.

By Brendan Coffey – Nov 28, 2026 at 2:40PM EST

Investors choosing between Docusign (DOCU -0.05%) and UiPath (PATH +1.85%) must weigh the stability of digital agreement leadership against the high-growth potential of automated business processes. Which stock is the better buy today?

Docusign transformed how contracts are signed, while UiPath automates repetitive tasks using artificial intelligence. Both companies are navigating a shifting landscape in which AI tools are redefining the utility of software. Comparing their financial health and market positioning helps determine which might lead through 2027.

Docusign provides its Intelligent Agreement Management platform and eSignature solutions to over 1.8 million customers. Its direct enterprise base includes 280,000 clients across industries like real estate and healthcare, supported by partners like Salesforce (CRM +0.51%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.60%). There is no significant customer concentration, as no single client accounts for more than 10% of revenue.

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached $3.4 billion, representing growth of about 8.6% compared to the prior period. The company reported GAAP net income of $329.9 million, resulting in a net margin of approximately 9.8%. This performance reflects a steady expansion in contract volume and the successful integration of its broader agreement management tools.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was about 0.1x, which compares total debt against shareholder equity. For investors watching tech stocks, the current ratio was 0.7x, a metric measuring the ability to pay short-term obligations with existing assets. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was $1.1 billion, though stock-based compensation (SBC) accounted for roughly 53.4% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

UiPath serves enterprise customers by focusing on automation and AI agents that orchestrate business processes. The company reported 2,565 customers with annualized recurring revenue of $100,000 or more, including partnerships with Snowflake (SNOW +3.20%). A substantial portion of revenue comes from its top 10% of customers, which indicates a level of customer concentration risk.

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue was $1.7 billion, showing growth of approximately 15% over the previous twelve-month period. GAAP net income reached $361.9 million, providing a net margin of about 21%. This growth is driven by increasing demand for automated workflows and agentic AI solutions in highly regulated industries.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the company had a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x, calculated by dividing total debt by shareholder equity. The current ratio of 2.5x measures short-term liquidity, suggesting the company has more than twice the assets needed to cover its upcoming bills. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was $352.2 million, but stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 78.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Docusign faces significant risks from competition with Adobe Systems (ADBE +0.84%) and potential disruption from generative AI language models. The company depends heavily on eSignature revenue, so failure to gain market acceptance for its new management platform could hurt financials. Cybersecurity threats and the unpredictable nature of long enterprise sales cycles also pose risks to its reputation and cash flow.

UiPath faces intense competition in the automation market from large platform vendors and smaller AI start-ups. Relying on a limited number of customers for a substantial portion of revenue adds significant risk to its long-term stability. The company also faces challenges integrating acquisitions and managing the reputational risks associated with AI inaccuracies or workforce displacement.

UiPath carries a lower Forward P/E and P/S ratio than Docusign, measuring market cap divided by sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

For Docusign, sales in its current fiscal year are seen growing by nearly 9% to $3.5 billion, with a slightly better percentage gain in net income to $346 million.

Docusign's launch and global expansion of its IAM platform, along with the introduction of AI-powered tools, should position the company for future growth. However, the not-so-great projected revenue growth rates suggest that Docusign may be entering a phase of more mature growth and a landscape of increasingly competitive digital agreement and contract management software. In particular, news reports that OpenAI would launch a ChatGPT product that would compete head-on with Docusign in the document summary field caused some investor fears. Right now, however, the signature and identity-verification part of Docusign's business appears unthreatened by ChatGPT.

AI is becoming a dominant theme in UiPath's business, with 18 of its 20 largest deals in its most recently reported quarter involving AI. The business raised its annual recurring revenue to more than $1.9 billion in its second quarter of fiscal 2027, up 13% year over year. Revenue in the quarter rose 13% to $410 million. For the full-year fiscal 2027, Wall Street analysts project revenue to rise 11% to $1.79 billion. Net income is expected to drop 30% to $200 million, while free cash flow is set to rise about 16% to $425 million, according to consensus estimates.

UiPath says that in the age of AI, its platform is about orchestration of enterprisewide software and systems to enable companies to find the efficiencies that AI promises while providing guardrails around AI and also working to ensure exactness--the idea being that even if AI is accurate 99.9% of the time, businesses like banks and medical providers need 100% accuracy. UiPath management says many businesses are deploying AI agents, but few have the connective tissue to link these single-task agents to the larger enterprise and to the multiple other software platforms they have deployed. UiPath says its software provides all that in a vendor-agnostic manner. That is its path to long-term growth.

At lower forward P/E and P/S ratios, UiPath is the choice for 2027.

#2874. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

#2869. Grant Nelson making impact amid Nets injuries

TORONTO — There is an NBA axiom about staying ready so one doesn't have to get ready. It's what Grant Nelson has been doing this season, really, the past two, with G League Long Island, awaiting his chance with Brooklyn.

That chance arrived with the Nets' big man woes that saw Nelson — who had five rebounds and four assists in a 124-100 loss to the Raptors on Friday — finally called up.

Brooklyn's struggles at the backup center spot, bottoming out with Moritz Wagner's knee injury, have given Nelson his opportunity. And he's cashed in to give the Nets some much-needed hustle.

"Just being [ready], staying ready, being out in Long Island under those coaches, just learning the system throughout the two years I've been here., being out in Long Island under those coaches, just learning the system throughout the two years I've been here. And when my name was called, being ready," Nelson said. "So, it's just great all the preparation that I put in, finally seeing that unfold on the basketball court. And it's just good to be with this team, get some minutes."

Grant Nelson walks down court during the Emirates NBA Cup Group Play against the Milwaukee Bucks at Fiserv Forum on Nov. 25, 2026 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Getty Images

Nelson, 24, got the call-up at the start of the Nets' four-game road trip, making his season debut in a brief cameo at Minnesota. But when Wagner, one of just two proven centers on Brooklyn's roster, left with knee soreness Wednesday in Milwaukee, that's when the 6-foot-10 Nelson had an opportunity to step up.

In the first meaningful non-tanking minutes of his career, Nelson actually helped the Nets to a 104-97 victory. He had just one point but added six rebounds, including three on the offensive glass, and was a plus-six in 13:04.

"You saw Grant: You plug him in, and he does everything well. His size, how smart he is, skilled, tough — really, really tough," head coach Jordi Fernández said. "And since we've had him here, he's been himself, and he's a very, very good basketball player. He was a big reason why we won. You see the rebounding and the activity and the physicality defensively, and I expect him just to play hard."

Of all the things Nelson did, playing hard was the most important. It's something that stood out on a Nets team that hasn't done it enough.

"He's just coming in and playing as hard as he can. He's not gonna be perfect and not make mistakes, but he makes up for it with effort," Julius Randle said. "He's just doing all the little things, the dirty work, the things that we need to win that might not show up on the stat sheet. So he's playing really hard, playing with a lot of good energy, and it's contagious."

Grant Nelson (16) and Egor Demin (8) play defense during the game against the Toronto Raptors during the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup on Nov. 27, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

For a Brooklyn team that has shown a disappointing lack of hustle and energy, Nelson provided plenty.

He led the team in Defensive Rating, Offensive Rebound percentage and box outs, with five of the latter. For perspective, the rest of the Nets combined for just six while the Bucks finished with seven.

Nelson was an undrafted 2025 rookie, and other than four NBA cameos he spent the season in the G-League working at forward and center. But this year he was exclusively a center, averaging 16.8 points and 11.8 boards on 57.4 percent shooting before getting called up.

"Continuing to work on my game, still making that transition to a five man, so being able to guard in the perimeter, still working on that jump shot. I've taken a step this year getting rebounds, so just doing that at this next level," Nelson said. "Just continuing to be able to guard ball screens, guard guards, being able to switch onto them when I have to. And then being in every action offensively and defensively, having the conditioning for that and being physical with the fives.

"How I move kind of gives me an advantage. So continuing to be able to move my feet defensively on guards.So continuing to be able to move my feet defensively on guards. … I feel like I still have a lot to work on, but just continuing to show that."

#2866. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis, an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. #2861. Houston Rockets vs. Philadelphia 76ers game preview

The Houston Rockets get an actual schedule advantage game tonight. After a few "Houston gets two days off and their opponents get one" matchups that technically favored the Rockets, the Philadelphia 76ers are coming in on the second night of a back-to-back after facing the Pacers in Indiana. Joel Embiid is questionable for that game and Jaylen Brown is out, which puts both on track to play tonight in Houston.

Philly only has one road loss as I write this, which is tied for the fewest in the NBA. The Rockets only have one home loss, which is also tied for the fewest in the NBA. So tonight is a game of strength. As the Rockets are in the middle of a five-game (and it could be six after Games 81 and 82 are announced) homestand, it continues to be important for Houston to win as many games as possible in the friendly confines of Toyota Center. As difficult as Houston's schedule has been so far, the Rockets have the tenth most difficult remaining schedule. The ten easiest remaining schedules all belong to teams in the Eastern Conference, even though I was told six ways to Sunday that the East was better than the West this season.

You already know the Sixers lineup, and Tyrese Maxey has seemingly taken the mantle as the go-to guy. He wrecked Houston last year in one of several "the Rockets led late but allowed their opponent to score every time down the floor when they only needed a single stop" contests. It was also one of Houston's many OT losses. That game was in Philadelphia, and Houston won the return matchup at home. Again, both teams look different now, but this is a game with a lot of starpower. It should be fun.

#2856. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.
